articles.title: From true contenders to tankers, ranking all 32 NFL teams by tiers entering the season
articles.summary: Which of the four tiers — True contenders, If everything breaks right..., Work to Do or Tankers — did your team land in?
articles.body:
Power rankings aren't the only way we can sort teams prior to the 2026 NFL season.

As any fantasy footballer worth their salt will tell you, linear rankings can tell you only so much. There might be a huge gap between the fourth and fifth best quarterbacks, or the seventh and eighth running backs, even if their names are next to each other on a list.

The same is true with measuring NFL teams' relative talent; there are dropoffs at different junctures. Instead, we're employing a tiered system indicating where teams are now based on talent, expectations and concerns. It's not a perfect system, but it's an interesting way to look at the league's big picture and see how the clubs size up, apples to apples.

Grouping teams into one of four categories doesn't mean that the top two are guaranteed a playoff run, or that the bottom two should plan on a long season — just ask the Seahawks and Patriots, two big climbers a year ago.

This is also not to say that every team within each category is on even footing. Rather, they're all lumped together with similar caliber strengths, weaknesses and unknowns.

Here's how we see the league stacking up prior to Week 1:

This tier is reserved for the best of the best. We're not talking unflawed teams here, but they're the ones with the most overall firepower to make deep playoff runs and potentially compete for a Super Bowl.

The Rams and Seahawks could be in their own tier, honestly, but that feels too elitist for a league that consistently churns over the top and bottom tiers on a nearly annual basis. Still, we're talking about the team that blowtorched the offseason — and which was just a hair behind the Seahawks a year ago — and the actual Super Bowl champs. And for the record, anyone sleeping on Seattle does so at their own risk. They're still in terrific shape for a title defense.

The Bills and Ravens took steps backward last season but still possess the QB firepower and all-around strength, even with coaching changes, to merit a spot here. The Eagles and Broncos might not have as much offensive heft, but their defenses and overall roster balance earn them rightful spots here.

The final two teams, the 49ers and Patriots, might not belong here on everyone's lists. But the 49ers won a road playoff game in the NFL's toughest division, despite being ravaged by injuries, and New England rode Drake Maye all the way to the Super Bowl. Flawed or not, the Patriots deserve respect and have a reasonable path back to the playoffs.

This next tier probably isn't that far below the upper group, but there are either more questions about these teams' stability or they possess one significant flaw that holds them back a bit.

Three of the four NFC North teams reside here, making up what might be the league's strongest division top to bottom. The Bears and Lions have the offensive firepower to be Super Bowl entrants, but can their defenses hold teams enough? The Packers might be slightly more balanced overall, but their defensive questions could linger until Micah Parsons' return.

The Texans and Chargers have similar makeups: strong to elite defenses, matched with offenses that don't always rise to the occasion on the biggest stages, making this a critical season for C.J. Stroud and Justin Herbert.

The Bengals and Cowboys each could be elite teams this season. Few are worried about them scoring, and all it might take to contend at high levels is moderate improvement defensively. Both clubs have pumped in resources on that side of the ball, so the potential is there.

The Chiefs reasonably could belong in the elite category, but last season's collapse — playing a tier below this down the stretch — and the uncertainty after Patrick Mahomes' ACL injury are reasonable reasons for pause. The Jaguars might be the toughest to slot of this group, coming off a nine-win improvement, but they were a very balanced team and deserve proper respect for that.

Truthfully, the Seahawks and Patriots likely would have begun last season in this category, so it's a reminder that there are no finished products entering Week 1 and no final judgements embossed on anyone. These teams all have elements that could result in contending seasons, but there are at least a few things with each that keep a lid on their potential until further notice.

The Bucs, Steelers, Vikings and Colts all had stretches last season where they were competent to very good contenders with some actual clout, but they all had incomplete seasons. With good health and more consistent quarterback play, each of them are capable of rising up the ranks.

The remaining teams in this tier have redeemable qualities and could outperform expectations. Can the Saints, Panthers or Falcons steal the South? All reasonable possibilities. Are the Giants or Commanders due for bounce-back seasons with better QB health and more defensive efficiency? Perhaps, with the right development and luck.

Atlanta's shaky preseason and big questions had me wondering whether the Falcons belonged here or one slot lower, but their elite skill-position talent was enough for them to hold steady here.

Of course no one is suggesting these teams are tanking on purpose. This is a tough category to find your squad residing in, but it's not purgatory either. It wouldn't be impossible for one of these teams to surprise this season.

The Raiders have upgraded at quarterback and are armed with young talent. There's excitement surrounding the Titans if Cam Ward takes a step up. The Jets had a strong draft class and got some key players back from injury.

The Browns have stacked two impressive draft classes together and might only need QB and OL stability to compete. The Cardinals and Dolphins are not devoid of talent, either.

It's just that these teams likely have the most hurdles to clear and the most big-picture questions surrounding them. Some are likely candidates for the QB derby in next year's draft, and you can't definitively say any of them are completely set at the position, which gives an indication of where they stand at the sport's most important spot.

articles.title: “Prepared 500 servings for 125 local families”: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies team up with Pete’s Garden, Shelter KC and FARE for Kansas City community impact
articles.summary: NFL News: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ charitable work through their 15 and the Mahomies foundation has addressed various needs across the Kansas City communit.
articles.body: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ charitable work through their 15 and the Mahomies foundation has addressed various needs across the Kansas City community, from food insecurity to food allergy education.Through separate partnerships with Pete’s Garden, Shelter KC, and Food Allergy Research & Education [FARE], the foundation has wholeheartedly supported families with meals, community resources, and practical, reliable information designed to make day-to-day life safer, better, and more manageable.The initiatives emphasize that access to food involves much more than putting a meal on the table. For some families, the challenge is food insecurity. For others, specifically those managing food allergies, navigating meals safely can require valuable education, public awareness, and trustworthy support.Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies foundation supports students while providing hundreds of meal servingsIn partnership with Pete’s Garden, the 15 and the Mahomies foundation supported a heartfelt initiative that brought culinary education and community service together back in April 2025.At Manual Career Technical Center in the Kansas City Public School District, culinary students sincerely prepared 500 servings of Lentil Ragu over Pasta for approximately 125 local families served by Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Kansas City.“When students realize they can cook a meal that feeds a community, something changes,” said Tamara Weber, Founder and Executive Director of Pete’s Garden. “By equipping educators with the tools and resources to lead impactful service projects, we’re building a movement of young leaders who understand the power of food to create change.”The insightful effort was part of Pete’s Garden’s Kids Feeding Kids program, which provides high school students with real-world, hands-on experience planning, preparing, and packaging family-sized meals.The service-learning opportunity also familiarizes students with serious issues surrounding food insecurity and food access within their own communities.The sagacious collaboration generated a dual impact: families received prepared meals, while young culinary students grasped real-world experience and a rare opportunity to use their developing skills in service of others.“Sitting down as a family to a healthy and wholesome meal is something Brittany and I really value,” said Patrick Mahomes.“But too many Kansas City families are struggling to get a wholesome dinner on the table. We are proud to support Kids Feeding Kids and help make mealtime easier for these families while also engaging students in a meaningful community service experience.”Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ Thanksgiving partnership with Shelter KCFor 75 years, Shelter KC has been a haven for Kansas City’s homeless men and women. In November 2024, Patrick and Brittany Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies foundation worked with them to support Kansas City families dealing with hardship during the holiday season.The foundation made a $15,000 donation to support Shelter KC’s annual Thanksgiving Family Feast.The contribution was wholeheartedly intended to provide Thanksgiving dinners for over 200 Kansas City families in need. Shelter KC and foundation volunteers were scheduled to prepare meal boxes and help create a celebration day centered on food preparation, building connection, and community service.The Thanksgiving partnership mirrored the foundation’s comprehensive commitment to supporting children and families through initiatives concentrated on health, wellness, and community resources, while also helping extend Shelter KC’s reach during the festive time of year. When nobody deserves to be sad or in need of wholesome food.“We are incredibly grateful to 15 and the Mahomies foundation for this support,” said Shelter KC Executive Director Eric Burger.“Their partnership is an inspiring reminder that we are all part of the same community, responsible for lifting one another up. This donation ensures that families who may be struggling this holiday season will have a Thanksgiving meal to enjoy together, and a renewed sense of hope for the future.”Brittany Mahomes brings food allergy education to Kansas City familiesFood-related support has also become a crucial portion of the foundation’s work through its partnership with FARE [Food Allergy Research & Education]. The joint initiative, known as “15 and FARE,” was established to expand food allergy education, support, and resources throughout the Kansas City area.On July 18, 2026, from 1 to 4 PM, “15 and FARE” hosted a free Back-to-School event at the Kansas City Public Library’s Plaza Branch for Kansas City-area families managing food allergies. The afternoon event included a Top 9 allergen-free school lunch demonstration, an Ask-the-Expert panel, a kids’ fun zone, and other health resources.The free open-to-the-public event was designed to help families prepare for the new school year while addressing questions that can arise when children with food allergies return to cafeteria lunches, classroom activities, field trips, and extracurricular programs where their parents or caregivers are not by their side.“As a food allergy mom myself, I know how important it is for families to feel prepared and supported, especially during back-to-school season,” said Brittany Mahomes, food allergy advocate and 15 and the Mahomies co-founder.“For parents managing food allergies, having access to trusted resources and a strong community can make all the difference. 15 and the Mahomies is proud to partner with FARE to bring Kansas City families together for a day of learning, connection, and fun.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Patrick Mahomes faces major Chiefs problem as injuries to Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy expose receiving corps concerns
articles.summary: NFL News: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs have a concern before their 2026 season opener: the wide receiver room. CBS Sports’ Jared Dubin ranked Kans.
articles.body: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs have a concern before their 2026 season opener: the wide receiver room. CBS Sports’ Jared Dubin ranked Kansas City 29th among all 32 NFL teams at the position, pointing to injury concerns around Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy. The Chiefs face the Denver Broncos on September 14, while Mahomes is expected to start after his knee surgery.Patrick Mahomes faces concern as Chiefs wide receivers rank 29thDubin’s ranking puts the spotlight on a group that has not had much stability. “With Rashee Rice still looking hobbled after rehabbing his knee injury in jail and Xavier Worthy again banged up in camp, the Chiefs might be counting on training-camp star Cyrus Allen to be a real factor, rather than a mere curiosity. That’s a dangerous game to play,” Dubin wrote for CBS Sports.Kansas City kept six wide receivers on its initial 53-man roster: Rice, Worthy, Tyquan Thornton, Jalen Royals, Nikko Remigio and Cyrus Allen. That leaves less room for proven depth if one of the main targets cannot play or is limited. The Chiefs had seven receivers in 2023 and 2024 and eight in 2025.Worthy enters the season with a chance to become a bigger part of the offense. He caught 42 passes for 532 yards and one touchdown last season despite playing through injuries. ESPN’s Dan Graziano has also pointed out that Kansas City had bigger plans for Worthy last year before a shoulder injury suffered on the third play of the season limited what the team could ask him to do.Xavier Worthy gives Patrick Mahomes a positive updateWorthy gave the Chiefs a reason to feel better on Wednesday. Speaking to reporters, he said he and Mahomes have spent the offseason working on their timing. “Me and Pat, we’ve kind of been working this offseason and obviously the timing and stuff you need to work on. . . . I feel like when it’s time to play, we’ll all be ready,” Worthy said, via NBC Sports.That connection could matter because Denver is the first test. The bigger news is that Mahomes appears ready to return. The Associated Press reported Wednesday that he has worked with the first team in camp after December surgery to repair torn ligaments in his left knee.Doctors had initially suggested October as a possible return, but Mahomes moved faster than expected. He did not play during the preseason, but that was planned. Chiefs coach Andy Reid said Wednesday, “He’s going to keep practicing just like he’s been doing,” while explaining that the team’s work before the opener will include more one-on-one practice.There is still an issue in front of him. Left tackle Josh Simmons remained out Wednesday with a back injury, while guard Trey Smith has been dealing with a hip injury. Kansas City has added depth on the line, but Mahomes could enter Week 1 with questions around both his protection and his receivers.For now, the Chiefs have a quarterback who appears on track to play and a receiving group that must prove the 29th-place ranking wrong.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel was 'in clear violation' of standards, The Athletic review says
articles.summary: The Athletic's standards review found Dianna Russini's relationship with Mike Vrabel violated company policy, raising questions about trust and disclosure.
articles.body: The Athletic has released a long-awaited standards review about former reporter Dianna Russini's relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and it paints the media entity as something of a trusting victim of a reporter who hid truth from her employer. The report does not attempt to conclude whether Russini had a romantic or physical relationship with Vrabel that helped her reporting through the years. But the report, authored by The Athletic's editorial director for standards and quality Mike Semel, ultimately decided that the company was uncomfortable with the relationship Russini had with Vrabel. THE ATHLETIC EXECUTIVE EDITOR ADMITS KEY MISTAKE MADE IN IN HANDLING OF DIANNA RUSSINI CONTROVERSY: REPORT "Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards," the report reads. "Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed." Semel believes Russini didn't use her platform to promote Vrabel. But he does not delve into the obvious possibility that the reporter used the relationship to help her own career. "I’ve not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to help promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic," Semel writes. "That said, there are examples of Russini writing glowingly of Vrabel that in hindsight are awkward or even uncomfortable." And let's be clear: The Athletic should be "uncomfortable" with Russini covering Vrabel "glowingly" because it raises an unspoken possibility of a quid pro quo exchange between the journalist and the coach that might help her work product The Athletic report cited only one story by Russini that "likely would not have happened were it not for the connection between Russini and Vrabel." The Athletic said its methodology in doing this investigation was extensive. It ... A source familiar with the report told OutKick that Russini did not speak with Semel for this report nor was her phone available for inspection by The Athletic. The report states that on April 7, 2026, Russini contacted executives at The Athletic and The New York Times Company to tell them of an impending Page Six article that would suggest a romantic relationship between her and Vrabel. She told her bosses the story would include photographs of the pair together, taken at a Sedona, Arizona resort. Russini apparently acknowledged a close relationship with Vrabel at that time, "but stressed that it was strictly professional," the report states. Page Six eventually published photos of Russini and Vrabel on the roof of a bungalow holding hands and embracing. It also published photos of the pair at a pool and at a hot tub together. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM It should be noted that The Athletic did not contact Vrabel in authoring this report. It did, however, speak with Russini's friends and colleagues within the company. The report does not specify if The Athletic asked Russini to provide exculpatory evidence that would alleviate concerns the company might have about a relationship it found in violation of its standards. And ultimately, The Athletic report makes it clear that Russini lost trust within the company because of the manner she handled the release of the New York Post's information. "[W]hen first confronted with the photos by The New York Post," Semel explains, "Russini waited two days before telling her editors and managers. She then told a story to explain the photos that did not align with facts, raising issues of trust." Vrabel has suffered no professional discipline from this episode, neither from the NFL nor the Patriots. Russini resigned her post from The Athletic months ago and even deleted her social media presence. She has not commented publicly about the issue beyond social media — at least not yet. articles.title: Athletic’s review of former NFL reporter Dianna Russini concludes she didn’t comply with standards
articles.summary: The report drew no conclusions about the nature of Russini’s relationship with Vrabel, who said he took accountability for his actions without addressing pho...
articles.body:
An investigation by The Athletic has concluded that former NFL reporter Dianna Russini violated the company's standards because of her relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel that led to her resignation in April.

The report drew no conclusions about the nature of Russini's relationship with Vrabel, who said he took accountability for his actions without addressing photos released of the coach and the reporter at a resort in Arizona. He stepped away from the team on the third day of the NFL draft to begin counseling and returned soon afterward.

"We neither completed an investigation nor reached any conclusion about the nature of the full relationship between Vrabel and Russini, but the totality of the public photographs are enough to conclude a violation of company policy," the report said.

Steven Ginsberg, executive editor at The Athletic, a New York Times-owned sports outlet, addressed the report in a message to employees Thursday.

"We undertook this review to ensure the integrity of our journalism and to maintain the trust our audience places in us. Nothing is more important than our credibility," Ginsberg wrote.

Mike Semel, editorial director for standards and quality at The Athletic, conducted the review of Russini's work, examining 903 stories, 204 episodes of her podcast and 77 videos.

"The review found that the vast majority of Dianna's stories were unrelated to Vrabel, and most of those that mentioned him did not raise concerns," Ginsberg told the staff. "We have, however, added editor's notes to four stories — one written and three videos — that did not meet our standards."

The photos of Vrabel and Russini were taken in Sedona, Arizona, before the annual NFL meetings that began in Phoenix on March 29, according to the New York Post. Vrabel and Russini are both married. The NFL did not investigate Vrabel's actions.

Vrabel led the Patriots to the Super Bowl in February, where they lost to Seattle. He was the AP NFL Coach of the Year in his first season in New England, finishing 63 points ahead of Jacksonville's Liam Coen.

Russini told the AP on Thursday that she stands by what she wrote in her resignation letter in April.

"I have covered the NFL with professionalism and dedication throughout my career, and I stand behind every story I have ever published. When the Page Six item first appeared, The Athletic supported me unequivocally, expressed confidence in my work and pride in my journalism. For that I am grateful. In the days that followed, unfortunately, commentators in various media have engaged in self-feeding speculation that is simply unmoored from the facts," Russini said then, adding she was stepping away "not because I accept the narrative that has been constructed around this episode, but because I refuse to lend it further oxygen or to let it define me or my career."

articles.title: 49ers, Rams hoping big-name players will be healthy enough to play in Australia matchup
articles.summary: Nick Bosa and George Kittle are among the players recovering from injuries who hope to be on the field in Week 1.
articles.body:
The San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams will open their seasons next Thursday in an historic matchup from Melbourne, Australia.

While the 49ers have already begun their trek down under, the Rams will not be arriving until a day before the game , which kicks off on Friday, Sept. 11, at 11:35 a.m local time.

As both teams prepare for Week 1, there are several lingering injury storylines to track. A number of key players are working their way toward being ready to play, but a few have yet to get a green light.

After tearing his Achilles in January, the tight end is trending in a positive direction as far as playing next week. Kittle practiced this week and, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport , there is an "optimistic sense" of the 32-year-old being available against the Rams. Like Nick Bosa, he was on the plane to Australia with the team on Wednesday.

The defensive end practiced fully for the first time in training camp on Wednesday, nearly a year after tearing his right ACL. He told reporters that he "felt great" and said the progress he is making is "very encouraging." As far as playing Week 1, he did not say anything definitive, but sounded like he was expecting to be out there next Friday (Thursday in the U.S.). Teams doctors will have the final say, of course.

"It was a long road," Bosa told reporters via ESPN.com . "There's some stuff I dealt with, with that patella tendon, and then I kind of ramped it a little too fast with the football stuff a month ago or whatever it was. And that kind of told me to back off. I've just been trying to get it as strong and myself as confident as I can to where I could rip the Band-Aid off and go to team stuff today."

The veteran receiver has been out for most of training camp with an adductor injury. He returned to practice this week. As with Kittle, there is optimism that the offseason signing will be ready to go next Thursday.

"We've got some solid work throughout the offseason," said 49ers general manager John Lynch on Tuesday. "He ran into a little hiccup with his adductor, but he's working really well to the side, and hope to get him back here early next week. And if all goes well, he'll be suiting up and making plays for us, and that's all the guy's done throughout his career."

The goal is Week 1 for the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year and current No. 1 player in the league . He has dealt with lower body soreness, and most recently knee swelling, that's kept him away from the field. Rams head coach Sean McVay said this week that Garrett is "making good progress" and the "goal all along has been [playing in] Australia."

The Rams receiver has been bothered by psoas soreness since mid-August, but made his return to practice on Sunday. The team has no concern moving forward and he is expected to be involved next week against the 49ers.

articles.title: From test cricket marathons to the NFL: Melbourne’s MCG readies for Rams-49ers
articles.summary: A debut Down Under has been a long time coming for the NFL.  It's fitting, too, that the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers will be playing their s...
articles.body:
BRISBANE, Australia (AP) — A debut Down Under has been a long time coming for the NFL . It's a good thing Aussies revel in the long game.

It's fitting, too, that the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers will be playing their season-opening game next week at the Melbourne Cricket Ground — known locally as the MCG or, more commonly, just as The G.

At 100,000 capacity, it's a big ground for a big occasion in a city that loves hosting big events. It's where for almost 150 years Australia has been playing test cricket matches, which can run across five days yet still finish without a winner, and it's the home of Australian rules football.

It has hosted the Olympics, Cricket World Cup finals, some of Taylor Swift's biggest shows and even a Papal mass.

Established in 1853, The G has developed a revered place in Australian sports and cultural life. Australia's premier venue will host the first of the NFL's nine international games this season .

The NFL ran a bid process across multiple Australian states for the debut Down Under and it was the MCG, being so cherished and so close to downtown, that sealed it. Along with Melbourne's success delivering high-profile events including the Australian Open — the season-opening tennis major at the adjoining Melbourne Park — and the Australian F1 Grand Prix .

"Melbourne as a city really stood out, having a huge stadium of that size, that caliber, that historical nature, in the middle of the city," Charlotte Offord, GM for NFL Australia/New Zealand, told The Associated Press. "It just felt like a bit of a no-brainer."

A cathedral, a colosseum ... it's not just cricket

Former Prime Minister John Howard, a self-described cricket tragic, once characterized the MCG as a place of worship.

In a 1996 speech at The G, Howard recounted how he'd mentioned to the Catholic archbishop that after visiting St. Patrick's Cathedral, "I was going to one of the spiritual centers, the true temporal shrine and sporting shrine, not only of Melbourne but also of Australia."

"Without any doubt the Melbourne Cricket Ground is the greatest sporting arena in our nation, and I think probably without comparison anywhere in the world."

It helps that Melburnians are renowned for a love of sport. It can create the kind of atmosphere at The G that cricket icon Dennis Lillee, the mustachioed and hairy chested fast bowler of the 1970s and 80s, compared with the ancient arena in Rome.

"To me the MCG is the people's ground,'' Lillee told Fox Sports before the Boxing Day test in 2014. It's not about the facilities, "It's the people. Even though the wicket was flat and the ball was old and dead, the crowd lifted you. They would go to watch ant racing. But for crowd involvement as an arena, a coliseum, the MCG was my favorite.''

It was a theme the late, great Shane Warne embraced, too. So much so that a big part of the homegrown cricket star's state memorial service was staged at the stadium in 2022 and a stand was renamed in his honor.

A week and many time zones away from that famous kiss with Travis Kelce after the Chiefs beat the 49ers in the 2024 Super Bowl, Swift told the crowd after three sold-out shows on her Eras tour at the MCG: "Melbourne, you are the love of my life. I cannot believe you, what you have done."

"Ninety-six thousand people the first night, 96,000 people the second night, 96,000 people tonight," she said. "All of that, those are all the biggest shows I've ever played on a tour and you did it three times!"

Swift's influence has helped grow the popularity of American football in Australia . Girls and young women account for a big proportion of the NFL's growing fanbase in Australia.

"I'd put that down to, one, flag football and girls playing," Offord said. "I'd also put it down to the Taylor Swift effect. We don't hide behind that at all — she has done great things for the league in terms of her ability to bring a new demographic of people into the fold."

The G has been home to Australian rules football since 1859, and has a pride of place in cricket history. Australia hosted England there in the very first official cricket test in 1877 — the forerunner to the Ashes contests between the two countries — and the first one-day international in 1971. The 1992 and 2015 World Cup finals were decided here.

It was the main stadium for the 1956 Olympics and the 2006 Commonwealth Games.

The MCG hosted baseball as early as 1888. In 1914, the New York Giants and Chicago White Sox played there.

While high-profile soccer, rugby union, rugby league and Gaelic football games have been contested at the G, American football's previous exposure to the venue has been limited. A 1908 game featuring teams from a visiting U.S. Navy fleet is one example.

As well as sports and concerts, the G has hosted the armed forces. In World War II, it housed a U.S. Army Air Forces depot called Camp Murphy, a regiment of the U.S. Marine Corps in 1943 and Royal Australian Air Force personnel.

American evangelist Billy Graham pulled the biggest crowd ever at the G — more than 130,000 in 1959. The biggest attendance for an Australian rules match is a touch under 122,000. By the mid-90s annual attendances for events at the MCG exceeded 3.5 million. The record aggregate crowd for a cricket match is 373,691 — across five days of the Ashes test in 2024.

Only Ed Sheeran has pulled a bigger concert crowd than Swift — his 107,243 in 2023 is the MCG record.

Situated in Yarra Park, the MCG is a 15-minute walk along the river to the city center and easily accessible by trams and trains.

The capacity is now 100,024, including 95,000 seated. The playing arena is oval shaped and is 174-meters (190 yards) at its longest length and 149 meters (163 yards) at his widest width. The rectangular NFL field will easily fit within the arena, but organizers say there won't be too much "dead space."

"We obviously have a lot of extra players that come with our game, (plus) cheerleaders, entertainment, equipment," Offord said. "You'll be surprised at (how little) space is actually left."

Will Bryce, head of the NFL's youth academy in Australia, said the MCG has an "aura you can just feel when you step in."

"It's going to be an incredible atmosphere," he said. "It's going to be a great collaboration between the NFL and everyone else involved."

articles.title: Grading Michael Wilson's $75 million extension to uplift Cardinals offense
articles.summary: Is Wilson ready to be a true WR1? Or was his 2025 breakthrough a product of circumstance that can't be duplicated?
articles.body:
The Arizona Cardinals hoped 2025 would be the year Marvin Harrison Jr. fulfilled his promise as a former top five draft pick. It was a different young wide receiver who rose up instead.

Wilson caught fire late in his third year as a pro. After a modest start, he put up a 119-catch, 1,600-yard, 13-touchdown full season pace after Week 11 for a Cardinals team in desperate need of playmakers. He finished the year with more than 1,000 receiving yards. While a good chunk of that can be attributed to a bad team trailing often and throwing the ball more than any other NFL team, it was still encouraging.

On Thursday, Arizona rewarded his rise. The Cardinals reportedly signed the 26-year-old wideout to a three-year, $75 million contract extension with $47 million guaranteed. It's a deal that will keep him in Glendale to see through another wave of his team's attempt to find a franchise quarterback. But was it the right move?

The deal: Arizona Cardinals sign WR Michael Wilson to a three-year, $75 million contract extension with $47 million guaranteed

Wilson was a pleasant complementary piece in 2023 and 2024. He looked to be locked into a similar role in 2025, but the transition from Kyler Murray to Jacoby Brissett helped spark a prolific finish to his third season.

Was some of that a Marqise Lee/ Jacksonville Jaguars "we're trailing and gotta throw the hell out of the ball in the second half" type opportunity? Certainly! But Wilson's underlying numbers suggest this is sustainable (and, also, Lee was pretty useful in 2017 when Jacksonville probably should have made it to the Super Bowl).

Despite playing with subpar quarterbacks, Wilson has recorded a catch rate over expected (CROE) of at least plus-4.5 percent in each of his seasons as a pro. He's had a positive yards after catch over expected (YACOE) in all of those years as well. He was a positive force on all three levels downfield, but made his biggest impact as an intermediate, chain-moving resource 10-19 yards downfield (plus-8.3 percent CROE, 9.8 yards per target and a ton of contested, Jacoby Brissett-bailing catches).

That's proof he can be an uplifting force for a flawed quarterback. And if there's one thing the Cardinals have lots of, it's flawed QBs. He can be the huckleberry for Brissett, Gardner Minshew II or Carson Beck this season. He can be the huckleberry of whomever the team drafts near the top of the first round in 2027.

He'll also help draw focus away from Harrison. The tantalizing prospect was largely inactive as Wilson rose to WR1 duties, but Harrison's seven target, six-catch performance in Week 13 helped show how these two can help each other. Then again, his average separation per target in games played alongside a surging Wilson was only about 1.6 yards, which suggests he wasn't getting open a ton despite having someone opponents needed to bracket.

So this isn't just a move that shores up the receiving corps; it's a reasonable insurance policy should Harrison never meet his potential. Wilson's $25 million annual average salary ranks only 20th among wide receivers. It's a proper bet, but not a franchise-altering one.

He probably won't average 1,600 yards per season over the life of that deal, but if he's even 85 percent as effective as he was to close out 2025 it will be an underpay. The only concern is the small sample size involved, which knocks this down from an "A" when Arizona could have waited to see if Wilson still had the juice, franchise-tagged him next spring and worked out a (more expensive) deal in the offseason.

articles.title: Giants' Cam Skattebo thought about retirement after season-ending leg injury: 'Do I really want to do this?'
articles.summary: Skattebo broke his right fibula and dislocated his right ankle in Week 8 last season.
articles.body:
Cam Skattebo said he thought about walking away from football after suffering a broken right fibula and dislocated right ankle in Week 8 last season.

"I would say the first month was kind of like, 'Damn. Do I really want to do this?'," Skattebo told "Up and Adams" host Kay Adams . "It was seven games. I was like, 'You know, I got to go back and play.'"

The New York Giants running back said that he entered the NFL last season with a mindset that if he ever experienced a major injury, he would retire. That wasn't the case as the 24-year-old is 100% recovered and looking forward to the team's Week 1 matchup against the Dallas Cowboys.

"Coming out of college, going into the NFL, I think I gave myself one rule, and it was if I ever got a major injury, I was done playing," Skattebo said. "And that happened seven games into my career. So, it kind of sucked."

As Skattebo made progress in his recovery, he was already eyeing the 2026 season. During a fan event in May, he told a crowd of Giants fans that he would be "ready to go" for Week 1 against the Cowboys and predicted a 300-carry, 2,000-yard season over 17 games.

In eight games last season, Skattebo rushed for 410 yards and five touchdowns, while also making 24 catches for 207 yards and two scores.

Skattebo said that the time away from the field not only helped him physically as he went through rehab, but also mentally with the amount of time he had to himself over the past 10 months.

"That gave me an extra step of finding that deep place, coming out of a hole that I didn't know I could come out of," Skattebo said. "I'm appreciative of that and I'm excited to see what I can build off of it."

articles.title: SEC sues LSU, alleging a coordinated push to recruit ex-pro athletes in defiance of rules
articles.summary: The Southeastern Conference filed a lawsuit against LSU and its leadership in Alabama federal court on Thursday, alleging the school had “waged a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes” against league rules.
articles.body: The Southeastern Conference filed a lawsuit against LSU and its leadership in Alabama federal court on Thursday, alleging the school had “waged a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes” against league rules. The extraordinary step against one of the league’s founding members in 1933 came as SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey testified 400 miles away in a courtroom not far from Tiger Stadium, defending the league’s ability to enforce its rules as several dozen athletes try to play this fall after they turned pro. Former New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Cleveland Browns tight end Dae’Quan Wright sat next to each other in the gallery as the hearing began, with Sankey taking the stand a short time later.. At least seven bailiffs were on hand. The lawsuit asks for a court injunction barring LSU from violating the SEC’s First Amendment rights by forcing it to “associate with conduct that is contrary to the conference’s purpose and mission.” It was filed in northern Alabama because the SEC is based in Birmingham. Attorneys for the athletes, the NCAA and the SEC were appearing before East Baton Rouge Parish Judge William Jorden, who scheduled the hearing concerning the status of his earlier temporary injunction preventing the NCAA from ruling recent former pros or fifth-year college athletes ineligible — a stance also taken by the SEC and other Power Four conferences with formal rules adopted last week. Jorden also wanted the NCAA to explain why it should not be held in contempt after the power conferences set up potential punishments of its member schools who place former NFL or NBA athletes on their football or basketball rosters. The players in question also include former Denver Broncos defensive back Blake Cotton, who like Harris and Wright is hoping to join LSU and new coach Lane Kiffin. Wright, who played for Kiffin last season at Mississippi, started practicing with at LSU this week, too late to be eligible for Saturday’s home opener against Clemson under the NCAA’s required seven days of practice. Harris, who also played at Ole Miss last season, has committed to LSU, while Cotton, who played at Utah last fall, has been recruited by Kiffin. All three are among a host of athletes who’ve argued in lawsuits around the country that they are unfairly being denied an opportunity to spend a fifth year in college under newly adopted NCAA rules allowing for five full years of competition. In all, the NCAA says there are approximately 450 athlete plaintiffs seeking additional eligibility through litigation, with some 300 of them winning the ability to play at least for now and about 150 who have been rejected. The athletes in the case who signed pro contracts have argued they did so only because current rules that would have allowed them another college season weren’t adopted until after their decisions to leave for the chance to make an NFL roster. The SEC filed a brief in the case on Wednesday in which it stated that the question before the judge should be a narrow one regarding whether the conference “can enforce and require its member institutions to comply with SEC rules.” The SEC’s proposed punishments include significant fines, up to half-season suspensions for coaches and member universities’ loss of voting on privileges on league business matters. Sankey provided an affidavit stating that SEC university presidents voted 15-0 in favor of the new rules, with LSU’s Wade Rousse abstaining. Sankey also said the SEC was acting on its own and not attempting to collude with NCAA to stop Kiffin from bringing in ex-pros. The fight over eligibility between schools and their own conference s and the NCAA has simmered for months and spilled into politics. Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr reportedly sent a letter of support to Sankey, encouraging him to take “all measures available” to punish LSU if it added former NFL players to its 2026 roster of 105 players, which was due to be submitted to the SEC by Friday. He also criticized the judge’s injunction. “It is no coincidence that the very institution set to potentially use this temporary order to flout the SEC’s rule is in the trial court’s own backyard,” Carr wrote. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill also weighed in, writing in a brief that the NCAA had subjected athletes in the case to a “classic bait-and-switch.” “The NCAA’s ever-changing rules have consequences beyond these individual athletes,” said Murrill, who attended the hearing and chatted with plaintiff attorneys before the proceeding. “They affect the universities that recruit them, the other student-athletes with whom they compete, and the coaches and administrators responsible for complying with an increasingly complicated set of rules.”

articles.title: Christian Gonzalez Responds to His Trainer Calling Patriots' Proposed Contract Language 'Trash'
articles.summary: Christian Gonzalez's trainer gave some insight into the cornerbacks' contract talks with the New England Patriots earlier this week, calling the language in the proposed deal "trash."
articles.body:
Christian Gonzalez's trainer gave some insight into the cornerbacks' contract talks with the New England Patriots earlier this week, calling the language in the proposed deal "trash."

On Thursday, Gonzalez didn't disagree with his trainer when asked about his comments.

"He can speak his mind. He's got his thoughts, I've got mine," Gonzalez said, per Karen Guregian of MassLive. "But I back everything he says. He backs everything I say. That's kind of our relationship. We talk every day. He's going to say what he's going to say."

Christian White, Gonzalez's trainer, said that the proposed deal from the Patriots would have made Gonzalez the highest-paid cornerback in the league, but the language wasn't what the star was looking for.

The Seattle Seahawks' Devon Witherspoon became the NFL's highest-paid cornerback last month when he inked a four-year, $132 million extension, resetting the market and paving the way for Gonzalez to earn even more when he reached a deal with the Patriots.

With the start of the 2026 campaign less than a week away, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Wednesday that Gonzalez doesn't plan to negotiate during the regular season.

"My understanding of this situation is that if Gonzalez were to sign a market-setting deal — and it will need to be just that — then it has to be buttoned up," Folwer wrote. "And the sides are not close on several elements of the deal."

The Patriots made it clear early in training camp that it values Gonzalez, with team owner Robert Kraft telling reporters that New England planned to give him a historic deal.

"We love Christian," Kraft said. "We love him as a player, as a person. That's why we've made an offer to him that makes him the highest-paid player to ever play that position in the NFL, and coincidentally, it's the highest contract in Patriots franchise history."

Gonzalez is entering his fourth season and has already proved he's worth the high price he's asking for. Last year, he had 69 tackles and 10 passes defended as he helped the Patriots reach the Super Bowl for the first time since 2018.

Asked whether he would consider sitting out the Patriots' season opener against star receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba and the Seahawks, Gonzalez was noncommittal.

"I mean, when that time comes, that's when things will happen," he said.

articles.title: New Fantasy Football 2026 Positional Rankings Printable Cheat Sheet and Top ADP Values
articles.summary: Opening kick of the 2026 NFL season is mere days away.
articles.body:
Opening kick of the 2026 NFL season is mere days away.

If you haven't settled on a direction for your fantasy football draft, what's the holdup?

Well, it might be due to a desire to collect as much information as possible before building that blueprint. So, let's gather more information for that collection with cheat-sheet style positional ranks and a couple of ADP values that could give you the ultimate edge on your opponents.

ADP Value: Jared Goff, QB, Detroit Lions

Ever wondered why seemingly every fantasy football expert recommends waiting on your quarterback? Well, the reason is now staring you in the face.

Without even investing a top-100 pick, you could leave your draft with Goff. And you'd immediately have a remarkably steady source of high-end passing production.

In each of the last three seasons, he has thrown for at least 4,564 yards with 30-plus touchdown passes. In the year before this streak started, he "only" delivered 4,438 passing yards and 29 touchdowns. He won't give you anything on the ground, obviously, but with aerial numbers like these, he doesn't need to.

He is a consistent high-floor option, but he might offer a bit more upside than normal this time around. He plays a fantasy-friendly schedule , for one, and he could see growth in his already electric collection of playmakers with the further development of Jameson Williams (and Isaac TeSlaa) and the return of a hopefully healthy Sam LaPorta.

ADP Value: De'Zhaun Stribling, WR, San Francisco 49ers

Stribling's stock has steadily climbed since the start of training camp. Despite all of this helium, though, it still isn't too high to make him a rather obvious value.

A lot of that has to do with him. He has a delectable blend of size and speed, and imaginations can run wild of thinking what coach Kyle Shanahan might do with physical tools like these. Stribling can be a field-stretcher, but he also has the elusiveness and burst to turn short passes into huge plays. Getting him in open space could be key in getting this offense its explosiveness back.

Some of Stribling's hype comes from the outside, too. Namely, the 49ers might wind up leaning pretty heavily on him due to a lack of reliable alternatives. Ricky Pearsall is out for the season, Mike Evans is 33 and already having trouble staying upright and Christian Kirk is on injured reserve. Looking past the receiver position, George Kittle is 32 and returning from a torn Achilles, and Christian McCaffrey is 30 and coming off of a 450-touch season.

San Francisco needs Stribling to be a productive piece of this offense, and it figures to give him every opportunity to serve as such. If he makes the most of his chances, Stribling could be a fantasy steal and maybe the Offensive Rookie of the Year.

articles.title: Texans' Kayshon Boutte Reacts to Mike Vrabel Saying He Would've Been 'Inactive' for Patriots Games
articles.summary: Over the weekend, New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel told reporters that wideout Kayshon Boutte "probably would have been inactive" had he remained on the team.
articles.body:
Over the weekend, New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel told reporters that wideout Kayshon Boutte "probably would have been inactive" had he remained on the team.

Instead, he was traded to the Houston Texans, and the veteran wideout responded to Vrabel's comments on Thursday:

"They did pay two guys to come in and do that job," he told reporters. "Sadly, it is the way it is. Being that it's a contract year for me, I [sought] a bigger role. I feel like what Vrabes said in his media interview, it wasn't nothing bad. I wouldn't say I'll use that as fuel... It was an honest opinion. He sat there, talked, [spoke] his truth, and [we'll] pretty much move forward from it."

The Patriots traded for A.J. Brown in the offseason, signed Romeo Doubs and brought back DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams and Mack Hollins. That left them with plenty of options at receiver, a major upgrade on the weapons Drake Maye had at his disposal last season.

It also made Boutte expendable. The 24-year-old was solid for the Patriots, with over 500 receiving yards in each of the past two seasons and a career-high six touchdowns in 2025. But with Brown and Doubs starting out wide and Douglas manning the slot, Boutte had more value to the Patriots as a trade chip than he did on the roster.

The Texans pounced, trading safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round pick to New England for the wideout. Houston had a major need at the position after Jayden Higgins tore his ACL.

"What I saw from Kayshon in New England; I saw a guy who's very competitive at the catch point, right?" Texans' head coach DeMeco Ryans told reporters after the trade. "Very strong hands, contested catches. He's coming down with the ball nine times out of 10. So, I saw that in his play, and that really stood out to me."

Boutte is now the frontrunner to start out wide opposite Nico Collins, and he seemingly hit the ground running in Houston.

"Kayshon's done he's done a really nice job of just diving into the preparation," Ryans told reporters. "[Wide receivers coach and passing-game coordinator Ben McDaniels] has been working with him since we were back in Carolina. So, he's been dialed in to his preparation, getting himself ready to go. He's out there running routes, lining, getting his plays done today. So he'll he'll be ready to go on game day."

articles.title: What did The Athletic really find about Mike Vrabel? Inside the Dianna Russini investigation and his “We’re moved on” response
articles.summary: NFL News: Mike Vrabel has made it clear that he does not want to revisit the controversy involving former NFL reporter Dianna Russini. After The Athletic releas.
articles.body: Mike Vrabel has made it clear that he does not want to revisit the controversy involving former NFL reporter Dianna Russini. After The Athletic released its findings on Thursday, September 3, the New England Patriots head coach was asked about the report during a press conference. Vrabel gave a short answer, saying, “We’re moved on,” before turning his attention to the Patriots’ upcoming season and their preparation for Seattle.What did Mike Vrabel say about Dianna Russini?Vrabel was asked about The Athletic’s investigation only hours after the report was published. He did not give his opinion on the findings and chose not to discuss his relationship with Russini.“No, I don’t have any reaction, no,” Vrabel told reporters. “We’re moved on,” he continued.Vrabel then made it clear where he wants his attention to be as the Patriots get ready for the new season.“We’re moved on and focused on Seattle and focused on the Patriots and focused on getting better this week,” he said.The reporter then asked Vrabel if he believed the situation with Russini was now fully behind him. Once again, the Patriots coach did not go into any details about the controversy.“I try to just say that I’ve moved on, and excited about this opportunity here as we start this season,” Vrabel said.His comments came as New England prepares for its season opener against the Seattle Seahawks on September 9. For Vrabel, the focus is now on his team and getting ready for the start of the 2026 NFL season.What did The Athletic’s investigation find about Mike Vrabel and Dianna Russini?The Athletic released its internal investigation on Thursday, with Mike Semel, the outlet’s editorial director for standards and editorial quality, overseeing the review.The report found that Russini’s relationship with Vrabel violated The Athletic’s standards because she did not disclose it to the company.“Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards. Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed,” Semel wrote in the report.The investigation did not establish the exact nature of Russini and Vrabel’s relationship. More importantly, the review did not find evidence that Russini’s reporting showed favoritism toward Vrabel or that he gave her information that other NFL reporters could not access.Semel carried out a broad review of Russini’s work. According to the report, he examined 903 stories published under her byline, along with dozens of videos and hundreds of podcast episodes. He also interviewed 14 members of The Athletic’s staff who had worked with Russini.The review found that Russini’s reporting was not mainly based on Vrabel. Her sources were spread across the NFL, and the investigation did not find signs that her work depended on her relationship with the Patriots coach.Still, The Athletic said the relationship should have been disclosed. That would have allowed Russini’s editors to decide whether there were stories involving Vrabel or the Patriots that she should not cover.“She did not,” Semel wrote.Russini resigned from The Athletic in April, shortly after photos of her and Vrabel at a resort became public. She has not returned to work since leaving the outlet.Vrabel, meanwhile, has continued with his job as Patriots head coach. With New England’s season opener approaching, he has chosen to leave the controversy behind and focus on his team’s preparation for Seattle.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley says opposing teams are learning plays from training camp videos taken by fans
articles.summary: Jeff Hafley knows how the Eagles stopped all his best play calls back in 2024.
articles.body:
The element of surprise can be a huge factor in any NFL game. A team that comes out with a unique strategy or formation can often win the day simply by confusing its opponent in the moment.

Unfortunately for Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley, he learned the hard way how difficult it is these days to catch an opponent off-guard. Hafley revealed Thursday that the Philadelphia Eagles were able to defeat his former team — the Green Bay Packers — in Week 1 in 2024 because Philadelphia had video of some of Green Bay's most critical play calls.

How did the Eagles obtain those videos? Fans at training camp, of course.

Hafley said Kevin Patullo — the former Eagles offensive coordinator who joined the Dolphins in the offseason — told Hafley the Eagles learned about the exotic pressures they would face from the Packers in Week 1 last year thanks to training camp clips taken by fans.

The Packers lost that contest 34-29 in São Paulo, Brazil.

Hafley's comment brings up a sticky situation NFL teams need to navigate in an era where technology makes everything more accessible. Teams undoubtedly want to hold opportunities in which fans can attend the occasional training camp practice, but need to hold back certain plays and coverages during those events, potentially resulting in a less exciting on-field product.

His comments also illustrate why so many teams seem to be using joint practices — not preseason games — as ways to prepare for the NFL regular season. Teams are more free to use actual in-game strategy in joint practices, which aren't televised and often come against teams they won't play in the regular season. Teams actually use their starters during joint practices, as opposed to preseason games, which seemingly feature fewer reps by starters each year.

As Hafley concluded at the end of the clip, there's not a ton NFL teams can do about it. Allowing fans to attend training camp is a way for teams to make money and increase excitement for the upcoming season. The only thing an NFL team can do to prevent actual strategy leaking to opposition is to not run those plays when fans are present. It sounds like Hafley will adopt that strategy moving forward.

articles.title: Bears' Caleb Williams Says He 'Fell in Love' with Chicago, Admits He Wasn't Sure He'd Like City
articles.summary: Chicago loves Caleb Williams.
articles.body:
The Chicago Bears quarterback appeared on the latest episode of Hot Ones and expressed his love for the city while handling a number of hot wings.

"I didn't think I was going to like it that much, to be honest," he said (1:45 mark). "And I fell in love with the city of Chicago. The people, the food, obviously the sports. I've got a couple other friends that are playing in Chicago sports. PCA. Matas."

PCA and Matas are Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs and Matas Buzelis of the Chicago Bulls. They are two notable names alongside Williams and Connor Bedard of the Chicago Blackhawks in a group of prominent young athletes who are all becoming household names in the Windy City at the same time.

Crow-Armstrong is on pace to be the National League MVP this season, while Williams led the Bears to their first NFC North title since 2018 and graces the cover of the latest edition of the Madden video game.

They're becoming two of the faces of their leagues simultaneously, and it is happening right as Williams falls in love with the city.

The Bears surely want him to be the face of the franchise for the next decade-plus, so his love for Chicago is welcome news for fans and the front office. He will be eligible for a new contract extension next offseason and recently said he is focused on far more than just money.

"Money's not a motivating factor for me in that sense," Williams said, per Jason Lieser of the Chicago Sun-Times . "If I wanted to be done today, I'd be fine. If I wanted to be done and go somewhere and disappear for a long time and never come back and y'all would never see me again, I'd be OK. That's not my motivation. Winning, winning, winning handles everything… so that's where my mind's at."

The Bears did plenty of winning last season in large part because Williams made a second-year leap under new head coach Ben Johnson.

He threw for a franchise-record 3,942 yards, led Chicago to a postseason victory over the archrival Green Bay Packers and is the primary reason there is so much optimism surrounding the team.

And more winning will only mean more love between Williams and the city.

articles.title: Former Lions, Broncos CB Alphonso Smith Jr. dies at 40
articles.summary: The former Wake Forest All-American spent four seasons in the league with the Broncos and Lions.
articles.body:
Content warning: This story contains a reference to suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide and needs support now, call or text 988 or chat with the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988lifeline.org .

Former Denver Broncos and Detroit Lions defensive back Alphonso Smith Jr. died on Wednesday, the Palm Beach County Medical Examiner's Office confirmed to the Denver Post .

Specifics of his death are not yet known. According to TMZ , Smith died by suicide in Pahokee, Florida, on Wednesday.

Smith spent four seasons in the league, first with the Broncos after they selected him with the No. 37 overall draft pick out of Wake Forest in 2009. Smith was dealt to the Detroit Lions after his rookie season in Denver. He immediately had his best campaign with his new team, and had 39 total tackles and five interceptions that season, including one that he ran back for a score.

In total, Smith had 87 total tackles and eight interceptions in his NFL career.

Smith spent four seasons at Wake Forest and earned All-American honors as a senior. He led the nation with eight interceptions in 2007, and followed that up with seven before he entered the draft. Smith was inducted into the school's Hall of Fame in 2022.

"First and foremost, I am heartbroken," Wake Forest Hall of Famer Jim Grobe said in a statement . "Alphonso was one of those special people that every time you saw him, he had a big smile on his face and he just made you feel better to be around him. And he was obviously a great football player, too. I just loved him and he was great to have on our football team. The team loved him, and he was a difference maker. He won a bunch of games for us and he made a lot of plays, especially late in the fourth quarter that turned games around and won games for us. He was an instinctive player. But, the No. 1 attribute I remember about Alphonso is his smile. He was a blessing for us."

Smith was cut by the Lions in 2012, and he returned home to Florida. He briefly served as the head football coach at Pahokee High School, where he went to high school, but was removed after allegations of inappropriate conduct, per the Denver Post. He was also charged with domestic battery after an incident with his former girlfriend in 2016, and there were roughly 19 incident reports made against Smith from 1999 to 2025.
