articles.title: 'If I can go through that, this is nothing': Packers WR Matthew Golden driven by a nightstand photo, bouts of homelessness
articles.summary: Getting drafted was a highlight. Golden told his teammates that when the Packers WRs each shared their three H's: hero, hardship and highlight. Golden's hero...
articles.body:
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Matthew Golden used to keep the photo on his bathroom mirror, next to the dry-erase list of goals he's scribbled atop mirror after mirror since he was 6 years old.

But now the Green Bay Packers' second-year receiver wakes up to the photo each morning on his nightstand. He glances at it.

Golden was young as he walked the aisle between pews, in his robin's-egg-blue suit. Perhaps 3 years old? At most, 5. Next to him, his cousin Makaylin's dress balloons from its blue velvet top into a white skirt with blue flowers. Golden was Granny's ring bearer; Makaylin, who was born the same day as Golden, her flower girl.

So much has changed since Matthew and Makaylin walked the aisle then, and so much changed long before the Packers selected Golden in the first round 23 years after they'd last spent a Round 1 pick on the position. Getting drafted, and achieving one of Golden's long list of mirror-scribbled goals, was a highlight. He told his teammates that when the Packers receivers went around the room in May to each share their three H's: hero, hardship and highlight.

Golden's hero and hardship? Those have shaped him much more strongly than his highlight.

First, the photo: Makaylin was killed not long afterward, in November 2009, when at 6 years old she was crossing her family's Houston-area street. A 62-year-old man who'd already received three DWI convictions was driving drunk, his blood alcohol level more than four times the legal limit, per a local ABC News archive . As he sped, he lost control of the car and flipped. Makaylin was killed instantly, on the street where much of Golden's family lived and where Golden and Makaylin had so often played.

Golden's "first best friend" — with whom he played with dolls and in the mud, and with whom he bickered over chicken nuggets and shared Chuck E. Cheese birthday parties — was gone in an instant. On the family street where she died, the heart-shaped brick memorial bearing her initials seemed to magnify the unfillable void as Golden aged while Makaylin didn't. The quiet but inquisitive Golden went from asking his grandmother questions like how many stars were in the sky and how far away the moon was to darker questions.

"The questions then turned to, 'Why did she have to die?'" Golden's grandmother, Penny Williams, told Yahoo Sports by phone this week. "It was, 'Because God chose her,' and that was the way we had to make him understand because he didn't."

Seventeen years after Makaylin's death, Golden still doesn't understand and still doesn't forget. He dedicated his "My Cause My Cleats" campaign last November to Mothers Against Drunk Driving, his cleats imploring "No More Victims." He grieves for Makaylin far more often than once a year.

"Obviously I was young and the more you grow up and you just go now with life, you kind of forget about those things," Golden told Yahoo Sports during a recent sit-down interview. "But for me, that never left my mind, just the way she was gone. I think about it every day. Especially during hard times when things do get rough.

"I just think back to just us being little kids and just going back to everything outside of football or outside life. And it was a special moment for me."

Golden thinks back to his early childhood when maybe things weren't easy but they also, when he turned 6, weren't nearly as hard as they'd become.

Because back when Makaylin pulled a stage-fearing Matthew down the aisle with her to throw flowers for Grandma Penny's wedding, Golden's bossy cousin's confidence offered a sense of security that in the coming years would dissolve.

The nightstand photo stirs emotions of Makaylin's loss — but also of the oasis of life back when Golden still only knew what life was like with consistent housing.

So when the Packers receivers went around the room in May, sharing their heroes and hardships and highlights, Golden told them of his mother, Alicia Blackshear, sacrificing to support her son physically and emotionally. And for his hardship, Golden explained: Growing up, Golden, his mother, grandmother and cousin had together experienced homelessness.

"We had a very dark moment for about seven years when we just couldn't come afloat," Blackshear told Yahoo Sports during a recent FaceTime interview. "But we went through it holding our heads high. That's what I wanted for Matt: I want you to be able to battle. Go toe to toe with anything that happens.

So as Golden returns for his second year in Green Bay after opportunities and production that disappointed his rookie year, he does not buckle at the pressure.

Golden didn't buckle at the pressure of the Packers bucking a decades-long trend to select him 23rd overall and he doesn't buckle at the pressure of rising expectations after the Packers moved on this spring from receivers Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks, setting him up for more targets.

Instead, Golden thinks back to the loss of his cousin and the bouts of homelessness and the strength his mother and grandmother modeled, and the pressure morphs into motivation, reinforced always by the work ethic his mother instilled.

"I just kind of think back," Golden says, and "I'm like, if I can go through that, this is nothing."

Sleeping in hotels and a Walmart parking lot 'pushed me to get to where I am today'

When they lived at a hotel, Williams shared a bed with her two grandchildren. Golden cradled his football each night; her granddaughter snuggled a Barbie.

Blackshear slept on the bed beside them. She worked two to four jobs at a time, but they never seemed enough to support and maintain housing for this blended family of four.

The bouts of homelessness began in 2017, when Golden's family lost their multigenerational family house for reasons Blackshear prefers to keep private. Soon came the challenge of finding a home — and the challenge of keeping it. As a teenager, Golden knew they were on the move but never knew exactly why.

"You're my child, I'm going to let you be the child," Blackshear said. "I'm not going to insert you into my adult life, my adult mess."

Instability followed, from hotel bills that surpassed $1,000 some weeks to a house that tided them over temporarily before paychecks from jobs at Kohl's, Sprouts, a trampoline park and a home healthcare company still didn't align in time to pay every electricity bill on time. An eviction followed, Blackshear's credit score sinking with it.

"It's hard to get out when you're in it, and it's hard to recover after…" Blackshear said. "Everything was steps, stumbling stones and just grace. The process, I mean, it'll humble you. And I'm not saying we were out there with cardboard boxes and signs begging for money, but we were without sometimes.

Dollar tacos and Lunchables became go-to meals. When hotel bills mounted, or home electric bills exceeded Blackshear's paychecks, they slept some nights in their car.

On those nights, which family members estimate lasted at least two weeks, Blackshear pulled her silver Nissan Maxima into the Brenham, Texas, Walmart parking lot and parked until 6 a.m. It was cold outside, but the car heat held. Blackshear and Williams took turns keeping watch as Golden and his cousin, who was under Blackshear's custody, dozed in the back. (Blackshear prefers that her niece, still a minor, not be named.)

"I was so young, to where it was: As long as I was with my mom, I was good," Golden said. "But at the same time I was like … why did it have to be us? Why are we going through this?"

Williams marveled at Golden's composure amid upheaval.

"Most kids would cry, break down and cry, get frustrated, throw temper tantrums, but Matthew didn't," she said. "He accepted what was going on, or at least we thought, because he never complained about it. And he would get so selfless and be like, 'Well, Granny, we only have one biscuit left. You take it.'

Football was a ticket to more opportunity.

Golden had shown a knack for the game from the time he was little, when he was about 5 years old playing with his Uncle Major, who was 15. Golden would encourage his grandmother to play catch with him, the duo undeterred by resulting urgent care trips to examine Williams' rotator cuff, knee socket and sprained ankle. Golden was fast, once winning a race for the fastest kid in his elementary school, Williams said. And he was stunningly driven at a young age.

"I didn't have a choice," Golden said. "Days I was just unmotivated and I just thought back to my family: 'I got to be the one to do it. If I don't do it, nobody's going to do it.' So I feel like having that mindset right there is really what pushed me to get to where I am today."

Brody Robinson noticed Golden first on the seventh-grade football field, when the kid in the high-top golden cleats was making plays that left him thinking, "Damn, this dude's nice." Basketball season came around, Robinson's specialty, and he again noticed the athlete when their schools competed. A mutual respect burgeoned, followed by friendship. As the summer between seventh and eighth grade neared, Robinson asked Golden: Will you join our 7-on-7 team?

Soon they were playing football and basketball together, sharing sleepovers as they became best friends. Robinson's parents would give Golden a ride to practices, at times picking him up in hotel parking lots.

Robinson estimates it was about three weeks before eighth grade when he asked his mom, Lisa McConnell: Could Golden live with them? She didn't hesitate.

Blackshear was conflicted but knew that Golden moving away was the only way to keep him in the school district as she worked to get her footing, her Brenham jobs 60 miles from the high school Golden would attend and even the closer hotels districted to Cy-Fair schools instead of hometown Klein Cain High School.

"As a mom you're thinking, 'Oh my God, I'm fixing to let my child go stay with some people. Oh, I'm a horrible mother,'" Blackshear said. "No. I had to really self-reflect on that moment and think about what would've been best over my pride."

Golden arrived to his new home with a single black trash bag of clothing and a pair or two of shoes, Robinson said. McConnell decorated Golden's new room, and a mirror in their house soon bore the dry-erase goals, from "NFL" to Golden's statistical and record goals changing by game and season. Dinners of the boys' favorite chicken alfredo followed, and the household gummy bear consumption accelerated quickly. Blackshear visited often: Robinson emphasizes how consistently mom was present in her son's life.

"That shows how much she really does love him and wanted the best for him, even if it hurt her," said Robinson, who now plays basketball for Creighton . "She made it happen as much as anybody else with sacrificing everything."

As Golden reached college stage, he leaned on faith but kept quiet

Golden's address changed throughout high school, from living with Robinson; to living with a man he now considers an uncle, Kevin Johnson; and then back with Blackshear, who had secured her own apartment by Golden's senior year, she said.

What didn't change: Golden's talent and production.

After a year on the freshman team, Golden raced to 3,242 yards and 32 touchdowns receiving in three varsity seasons. He rose to a four-star recruit and the 27th-ranked player in the state's class of 2022, per Rivals . Golden stayed close to home, signing with Dana Holgorsen to play for the University of Houston.

Golden posted 584 yards and seven touchdowns in his first year, breaking Houston's true freshman receiving touchdown record while rounding into form with two 100-yard games in the last five contests.

As a sophomore, moving between the outside receiver and slot positions, Golden scored six receiving touchdowns and two return touchdowns in nine games. His 725 all-purpose yards ranked second on the team even as he missed the final three games due to turf toe.

The surgery, paired with the firing of Holgorsen, tested Golden. Football had been his consistent outlet through the pain of grief and the fear of where he'd sleep. No longer.

But Blackshear had long preached faith: "It ain't your job to understand why it happened. It's your job to make it through it and come out on the other side." Golden leaned into scriptures and motivational messages, saying he felt closer to God as he rehabilitated. He transferred to Texas.

There, Longhorns coaches believed he was a good route-runner with extremely strong hands and a toughness to run through contact. They valued his position flex while also holding him to a high standard as he transitioned from Houston's Air Raid system to Texas' pro-style offense complete with formation and motion responsibility.

"I told him I wasn't giving away a starting spot, that it was going to be earned," Longhorns passing game coordinator and wide receiver coach Chris Jackson told Yahoo Sports. "He said, 'I'll never forget that.' He goes, 'I needed to hear that.'

"He just went about his business to prove himself right."

Golden proved himself right with a one-handed touchdown catch against Vanderbilt and he proved himself right with a game-high 149 yards in a College Football Playoff quarterfinal win against Arizona State. The crunch-time performance: Golden scored a 28-yard touchdown on fourth-and-13 in overtime to tie the Sun Devils, later muscling for the contested catch on the 2-point conversion that sealed the win.

He performed. But he didn't open up about the hotels nor the Walmart parking lot.

"It's strictly business," Blackshear said. "So that doesn't mean me airing out my life for you guys to feel closer to me. That's how I took it. …

"I said, 'Son: You don't let nobody question your mannerism. Just because you're not smiling all up in their face every day doesn't mean that you're not going to go out on the field and produce. … I would tell him you don't have to share, but you do have to move with respect."

Golden declared for the draft, projecting as a versatile receiver who'd embraced outbreaking routes from the slot in the red zone and became fond of 14-yard stop routes using different play speeds, Jackson said. NFL talent evaluators saw him as a No. 1 to No. 2 wide receiver with speed, ball skills and route-running chops; they were impressed by his contested-catch ability relative to his 5-foot-11, 195-pound frame.

And when Golden beat all his receiver classmates with a 4.29-second 40-yard dash at the scouting combine? His stock rose further, his mirror-scribbled dreams materializing before his eyes.

Williams asked Golden what was going through his mind as he raced.

"He said, 'I'm running home to my granny,'" Williams said. "So I asked Alicia, I said, 'Alicia, what did he tell you?'

As Jordan Love predicts 'big year' from Golden, Golden hopes he inspires more than just football fans

While the lore of the 23-year gap between first-round Packers receivers is fair, it's perhaps more public than other teams' drafting trends because of quarterback Aaron Rodgers.

Two receivers drawing Packers interest, Brandon Aiyuk and Justin Jefferson, went within four spots of quarterback Jordan Love in 2020. Rodgers famously responded to Green Bay drafting his successor rather than a weapon for him by winning consecutive MVP titles. So yes, Golden marked the first receiver Green Bay took in the first since they selected Javon Walker 20th overall in 2002. But Packers brass hear the chants and want to contextualize: They selected seven second-round receivers in that stretch and three more in the third.

"It's never been philosophical," general manager Brian Gutekunst told Yahoo Sports in May 2025. "But at the same time, we've always known you can get good receivers later. [Golden] just happened to work out for us."

Golden caught the Packers' eye not only because of his versatility but also, and meaningfully, because they believed he could thrive outside. They appreciated that he did not need to carry the room right away while working alongside Christian Watson, Jayden Reed, Doubs and Wicks. Tight end Tucker Kraft and running back Josh Jacobs, entering Golden's rookie year, also were sure to get touches.

The result: Golden caught 29 of 44 targets for 361 yards in the regular season. He flashed with plays, including a chain-mover on fourth-and-6 in overtime against the Dallas Cowboys and as he adjusted to beat safety Jordan Battle for a deep ball on third-and-9 against the Cincinnati Bengals.

But shoulder and wrist injuries sidelined Golden three games. Adjusting to a complicated scheme with touches sparse in a deep room slowed his takeoff. Love talked with Golden often, quarterback reminding receiver about the three years that Love had sat behind Rodgers before starting. Love's vote of confidence helped Golden's psyche some. Still, when the playoffs began, Golden had not scored a touchdown.

"That was one of those things that was just kind of hanging over the whole season," Love told Yahoo Sports in July. "Every game's, 'We're going to get you one this game. We're going to get you one.'"

In a wild-card matchup against the Chicago Bears, they finally did.

Up 21-16 in the fourth quarter, Love hit Golden in the backfield and let his receiver work from there. Golden evaded four initial defenders, spinning out of one's tackle and hurdling another before ignoring the grasp of a third. He barreled into the end zone for a 23-yard score that featured 29 yards after the catch.

A wave of relief washed over Golden. In the stands, Blackshear cried.

"I feel like that one touchdown gave him so much clarity after not getting any all year," Blackshear said. "Everybody else seen, 'Oh touchdown. Oh well, go team go.' No. When we celebrated, it was celebrated more because we knew the impact that it was going to have on his mental."

The nine months until Golden's next opportunity now stood against the backdrop of his postseason 84 yards and touchdown rather than the burden of his end zone-less rookie debut.

When training camp arrived, that momentum was evident.

In July 30 team drills, Love found Golden early and often. Love's explanation: While the Packers' system values staying true to quarterback reads, Golden is playing outside more now, a position that's heavily featured in Love's progressions. Nearly a month later, in a joint practice against the Cardinals, Love praised Golden for his route and catch in a narrowing window on a touchdown against safety Budda Baker.

Teammates believe these highlights will become increasingly routine now that Doubs and Wicks left after a combined 131 targets last year. Golden's opportunities outside should expand, too: While Golden took just 267 of his 488 offensive snaps (54.7%) at wideout last year, per Pro Football Focus data, Doubs took 708 of 831 (85.2%) and Wicks, 197 of 410 (48.0%).

Doubs' 8.5 yards per target last season weren't far from Golden's 8.2; but with 85 targets to Golden's 44, Doubs posted 724 yards and six touchdowns.

"The X position in our offense is someone who, you get a lot of targets," Love said. "You can see our connection already picking up where it left off and him able to step in that role where really [Doubs] was at X last year for the majority.

"I think he'll be able to take over that position and have a big year."

Golden hopes any big year inspires much more than just himself and his teammates.

Williams remembers sitting on a couch with her grandson after he began sharing his story at the NFL Draft. She asked: Why did you tell people? Weren't we going to keep this our secret?

"He said, 'Granny, because [there's] a lot of people in the world [who are] homeless,'" Williams told Yahoo Sports by phone this week. "'And I just want somebody that think they can't make it [to know] that they can make it.'"

Williams says Golden added: "It was scary, Granny."

"He said, 'Because I had to be brave for y'all,'" Williams said. "He just didn't want us to know that he was scared."

The fear of homelessness has since dissipated, from Blackshear finding stability late in Golden's high school days to Golden teaming up with with RE/MAX to gift Williams a new house . Golden's first-round contract amounted to $17.57 million fully guaranteed at signing. He's financially more secure, but the impact of his heroes and hardships continue to define him.

So Golden will keep waking up to Makaylin's photo on his nightstand and to the dry-erase goals on his mirror, the "NFL" goal still written as a reminder of how far he still wants to go.

But now Golden wakes up in the same home each morning in Green Bay, writing on the same mirror rather than a hotel mirror here and a car side mirror there. And he wakes up knowing he no longer hides his past. Sharing his "three H's" with receivers in May, he found comfort in the vulnerability.

"That's what puts just the heart and just the fire I have behind my character the way I am," Golden said. "A lot of people growing up, they always told me I seem unapproachable or kind of got an ego, but it's never been that. It's always been strictly when I'm playing football, it's business to me. I'm trying to get somewhere. I got a goal I'm trying to reach. I just feel like for me, once people talk to me and they get to know me, they'll understand why.

"And for me, that's why I started letting my story be known. …

"That's really the reason I am the way I am."

Jori Epstein is a senior NFL reporter for Yahoo Sports and the author of 'The Upstander: How Surviving the Holocaust Sparked Max Glauben's Mission to Dismantle Hate.' She previously reported for USA TODAY and The Dallas Morning News. Follow Jori on Twitter @JoriEpstein.

articles.title: Cam Skattebo considered retirement after season-ending ankle injury in Giants rookie year
articles.summary: Cam Skattebo revealed retirement crossed his mind after a devastating ankle and leg injury just eight games into his New York Giants rookie season.
articles.body: Cam Skattebo’s first season in the NFL with the New York Giants was going swimmingly — until it ended in one play. Skattebo suffered a season-ending ankle injury just as his production, and subsequent stardom, was rising in the league. Alongside Jaxson Dart, the new era of Giants had proven they can go against some of the best teams in the league. But when Philadelphia Eagles linebacker Zack Baun’s tackle at Lincoln Financial Field in Week 8 ended with a dislocated right ankle and open fracture of the right tibia for Skattebo, he was distraught. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM In fact, he told Kay Adams on "Up and Adams" that retirement even entered his brain after just eight games with the Giants. "Yeah, definitely," he responded to the host when asked. "The first month was kind of like, ‘Damn, do I really wanna do this?’" SUPER BOWL CHAMPION PARRIS CAMPBELL RETIRES FROM NFL AT 28, COWBOYS ANNOUNCE The shock of a season abruptly ending due to injury can do more than physical damage to a player. The mental fortitude needed to recover is just as important, and Skattebo eventually found it. " It was seven games, I was like, ‘I got to go back and play.’ Yeah, there’s no shot. There’s no different story. No, it was the end of the year and I was like, ‘OK, I’m over this,’ you know, and I didn’t feel that way at all." But Skattebo, after a tremendous final year at Arizona State that put him on the NFL radar, made himself a rule for when he turned pro. "Coming out of college, going to the NFL, I think I gave myself one rule and it was if I ever got a major injury, I was done playing," he said. "And that happened seven games into my career. So, it kind of sucked." Skattebo eventually found the inner strength needed to battle through his injury and its recovery. CAM SKATTEBO'S BACKFLIPPING AT FANATICS FEST REPORTEDLY EARNED HIM A TALKING-TO FROM GIANTS "I think that really helped me find who I am as a player and as a person," he explained to Adams. "I was able to sit at home for 14 hours a day, do absolutely nothing for weeks on end. So just finding who I was, finding my happiness, finding the person I wanted to be on and off the field. And I think that’s something that I’ve built over the last nine, 10 months." Skattebo enters the 2026 season hoping to get back to his bulldozing self in the Giants’ backfield, which now features Najee Harris as well as Tyrone Tracy and Devin Singletary. New offensive coordinator Matt Nagy seems to want to use all his running backs in a committee, but Skattebo proved to be someone that will go the extra mile to get first downs and cross the goal line — even if he’s carrying some defenders with him. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The fourth-round pick finished with 410 rushing yards on 101 attempts with five rushing touchdowns, while hauling in 24 passes for 207 yards and two more scores across eight games.

articles.title: Alphonso Smith, 2-time All-America DB who played in the NFL for 4 seasons, dies at 40
articles.summary: Alphonso Smith, a two-time All-America defensive back who played in the NFL for four seasons, has died.  Smith died on Wednesday, according to Wake Forest, w...
articles.body:
PAHOKEE, Fla. (AP) — Alphonso Smith, a two-time All-America defensive back who played in the NFL for four seasons, has died. He was 40.

Smith died on Wednesday, according to Wake Forest , who was informed by his family. No cause of death was given.

Smith appeared to post on his Facebook account on Wednesday, lamenting his mental health challenges, apologizing and asking for forgiveness.

"Do not cry for me!" a post read on his account. "I tried everything in my power to fight the demons behind the ones that someone put into ME! I did not want to be that WAY! I know I have disappointed so many folks. This is a DEMON in me! But not only me! It's EVERYONE! I have HURT so many! I needed help & did not get it! I am so sorry!"

Smith apologized to his children in the note and suggested that trauma from his childhood had caused him mental anguish. "I pray my soul rest in heaven for my heart is pure," he said.

Denver drafted the former Wake Forest star in the second round of the 2009 NFL draft. After playing in 15 games for the Broncos, returning punts and kickoffs, he was traded to Detroit shortly before the 2010 season.

Smith played in 33 games, including 11 starts, over the next two seasons with the Lions and had eight interceptions, returning two for touchdowns.

The Lions released him just before the 2012 season, signed him later that year and cut him again after he played in four games as a backup.

Smith went to Pahokee High School in his hometown, where he helped the football team win a Florida state title as a two-way star playing quarterback and defensive back in 2003. He redshirted as a freshman at Wake Forest and went on to become a key player for the program over the next four seasons.

Smith was a first-team Associated Press All-America defensive back in 2008 and a third-team All-America in 2007.

After playing in 44 NFL games over four years, he worked as a sideline reporter for Wake Forest football games during the 2013 season when he was also an assistant high school coach in nearby Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

Smith was a head high school football coach in Moore Haven, Florida, and Pahokee High School, where he was also dean of students in charge of discipline, according to his LinkedIn account. His last listed job was director of marketing for a South Florida family physician.

articles.title: Mike Tomlin Teases Potential for NFL Return After Taking TV Role with NBC Following Steelers Exit
articles.summary: Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach and current NBC Sports analyst Mike Tomlin isn't ruling out a return to coaching at some point in the future.
articles.body:
Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach and current NBC Sports analyst Mike Tomlin isn't ruling out a return to coaching at some point in the future.

"I don't know about the long-term component of things," he said during an appearance on The Rich Eisen Show Thursday (2:00 mark). "I've just lived enough to know to leave certain doors ajar. But man I gotta admit, my pulse rate is pretty low these days. I've enjoyed my summer home to the fullest. It's been a good offseason."

Tomlin, 54, spent 19 seasons as the head coach of the Steelers, leading the team to a 193-114-2 record, 13 playoff appearances, two Super Bowl berths and one championship. While Tomlin never posted a losing record in Pittsburgh, the Steelers also haven't won a playoff game since the 2016 season.

Now he's moved to the broadcasting role, and he doesn't seem keen on speculating about his future before his media career has barely begun:

But coaching is something that he clearly hasn't ruled out entirely going forward.

articles.title: Will Levis Tries Out for Jets After Titans Release, Eyes Role on QB Depth Chart
articles.summary: Former Tennessee Titans quarterback Will Levis tried out for the New York Jets on Thursday, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter.
articles.body:
Former Tennessee Titans quarterback Will Levis tried out for the New York Jets on Thursday, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter .

Levis was a member of the Titans throughout the past three seasons before he was waived on Sunday.

The Jets only kept two quarterbacks on their 53-man roster, with rookie Cade Klubnik backing up veteran Geno Smith.

He opened his rookie season as a depth option before ultimately starting in nine games, completing 58.4 percent of his throws for 1,808 yards and eight touchdowns compared to four interceptions.

Although Levis entered his 2024 campaign as Tennessee's starting quarterback, he struggled mightily. In 12 games, he threw for 2,091 yards and 13 touchdowns while getting picked off 12 times. He also lost six fumbles.

Levis will now look to join a Jets squad that's attempting to improve upon a 3-14 finish in 2025.

articles.title: D'Andre Swift, Rome Odunze Injured at Practice, Latest on Bears Stars Ahead of Week 1 vs. Panthers
articles.summary: The Chicago Bears received some tough injury news during Thursday's practice, as running back D'Andre Swift and wideout Rome Odunze each suffered injuries ahead of a Week 1 matchup with the Carolina Panthers on Sept. 13.
articles.body:
The Chicago Bears received some tough injury news during Thursday's practice, as running back D'Andre Swift and wideout Rome Odunze each suffered injuries ahead of a Week 1 matchup with the Carolina Panthers on Sept. 13.

The Bears have already been managing a knee injury to running back Kyle Monangai, making any injury to Swift all the more concerning.

Odunze, fortunately, is expected to be "all good" after initial testing, per Dan Wiederer of The Athletic.

Swift, 27, led Chicago's backfield last season, rushing for 1,087 yards and nine touchdowns in Ben Johnson's run-heavy attack while adding 34 catches for 299 yards and another score. Monangai provided the boom stick, adding 783 yards and five scores on the ground.

If neither is ready to go for the season opener, Roschon Johnson would be next in line to lead the backfield.

The 24-year-old Odunze, meanwhile, only appeared in 12 games during the 2025 season but did register 44 catches for 661 yards and six touchdowns. With D.J. Moore traded in the offseason to the Buffalo Bills, Odunze, Luther Burden III and tight end Colston Loveland are expected to highlight the team's passing attack.

Odunze raised some eyebrows in the summer when he told reporters that last year's foot injury and the nature of that break created a "new normal" for him going forward, though he later clarified those remarks.

"I really didn't articulate it well, honestly. That's not really what I meant," he told reporters . "I just kind of meant that I had an injury. That's it. That's football. My foot feels great. My foot feels amazing. The training staff here, the training staffs I work with in the offseason, all the work that I've put in to get it right, honestly it's not even really something that I think about anymore which I think is the best thing I think you can have after an injury. I know 'new normal,' that has a bunch of connotations of chronic and severe, like it's never going to be the same. It's not like that at all. I'm completely fine. I went through my process of recovery and rehab, and it's been great. Obviously I do my due diligence and all those things. Being out sucks. That really is the No. 1 thing as a football player, any athlete, you all know, you don't want to be out—practice, game, whatever it is. Went through my process of getting that right, and I feel amazing."

Still, last year's injury issues makes Thursday's development a nervy one for the Bears as they look to replicate last year's playoff appearance and take the next step as a Super Bowl contender.

articles.title: Mark Sanchez files guilty plea for charges related to stabbing incident in Indianapolis
articles.summary: The former NFL quarterback-turned-analyst was arrested in October 2025 after allegedly assaulting a truck driver while intoxicated.
articles.body:
Former Fox Sports analyst Mark Sanchez will plead guilty to charges relating to an altercation from last fall, according to Indiana court records. Sanchez, who was facing three misdemeanors and a felony battery charge, filed a motion for a guilty plea on Thursday.

In October, Sanchez was stabbed in Indianapolis after allegedly sparking an altercation with a truck driver while intoxicated. He was initially charged with three misdemeanors — battery, unauthorized entry of a motor vehicle and public intoxication — and later charged with a felony for battery resulting in serious bodily injury.

It is unclear which of the charges Sanchez is pleading guilty to. Sanchez's attorneys are reportedly requesting that his sentencing hearing take place on Nov. 9 or Nov. 16 if his plea is accepted, per multiple reports.

Sanchez's jury trial was originally set for March 12, but was rescheduled at least five times, most recently to Sept. 8.

Sanchez, a former New York Jets quarterback-turned-analyst, was fired by Fox a month after the incident.

Perry Tole, the truck driver who Sanchez allegedly assaulted, also filed a civil lawsuit against Sanchez and Fox.

Sanchez charged with battery after altercation

The incident took place early in the morning on Oct. 4, the day before Sanchez was set to call the NFL's Week 5 matchup between the Indianapolis Colts and Las Vegas Raiders on Fox Sports.

Security footage of the incident , which officials later said matched Tole's account, showed Sanchez following Tole into an alley and confronting the 69-year-old truck driver. Tole told police that Sanchez smelled like alcohol and was slurring his speech, and said that he felt physically threatened as the confrontation escalated.

After arguing with Tole, Sanchez allegedly climbed into Tole's truck. A fight began when Sanchez allegedly threw Tole against a dumpster; the truck driver said he defended himself with pepper spray before pulling out a knife. Tole said he stabbed Sanchez in the chest in self-defense, while Tole sustained a large gash in his cheek during the fight.

Sanchez was released from the hospital a week after the incident and booked in Marion County jail.

In his first public comments, he said that he was "focused on the recovery" and said it would be a "long process." Sanchez initially pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Former Fox Sports analyst Mark Sanchez plans to plead guilty rather than go forward with a trial next week stemming from an October 2025 fight with a truck driver outside an Indianapolis hotel, according to court records filed Thursday.

The motion asks Marion County Superior Court to schedule a hearing for Sanchez to plead guilty and be sentenced. Online records did not indicate which charges he plans to plead guilty to.

"This is a positive development. We are finalizing an agreement with the prosecutor's office that provides a path toward resolving the state's case. Atwell then signed with the Miami Dolphins, though the Rams made a surprising trade in late August, reacquiring Atwell for running back Jarquez Hunter to fill their No. 3 receiver need.

"Nah, man, it don't feel like I was gone," Atwell told reporters on Thursday. "I'm back with my brothers, man. I just feel great and feel awesome just to be back here and with these great players and guys. I'm just excited."

Atwell, 26, set career highs in receptions (42) and receiving yards (562) in 2024 but his playing time and production fell off last season (six catches for 192 yards and a score) as he fell behind starters Puka Nacua and Davante Adams and backups Jordan Whittington, Konata Mumpfield and Xavier Smith in the pecking order.

All five are back in Los Angeles. But the Rams clearly felt Atwell still had something to offer their offense.

"I just take it one day at a time—you know, do what I do and what I can control," he told reporters. "At the end of the day, [head coach Sean McVay] has always got a plan, whether it's for me or the team or whatever it is. You know he's going to put us in the right position to play good and execute the play. Overall, when my number's called, I just make the best of that moment."

articles.title: Michael Lombardi resigns as North Carolina football GM amid school investigation
articles.summary: North Carolina football general manager Michael Lombardi has resigned, ending the tenure of an immediate hire in Bill Belichick’s NFL-to-college coaching tra...
articles.body:
North Carolina football general manager Michael Lombardi has resigned, ending the tenure of an immediate hire in Bill Belichick's NFL-to-college coaching transition who had been on on paid administrative leave as the subject of a school investigation .

The school announced Lombardi's resignation Thursday. It also stated it would continue its ongoing investigation and "consider all appropriate corrective actions" as needed.

The school has not released specifics of that probe, noting in its July 27 announcement that employees and athletes aren't permitted to address the topic "as is standard procedure with personnel matters." Three days later, UNC released another statement that said its Office of University Counsel was conducting an investigation, an announcement coming on the first day of preseason camp.

Two people with knowledge of the situation previously told The Associated Press that a human resources complaint from a former employee was involved. They spoke on condition of anonymity because the school wasn't publicly discussing case details.

Attorney Tom Mars, who is working with Lombardi, released a statement from his client confirming the resignation Thursday.

"I want to thank Chancellor (Lee) Roberts and Bill Belichick for the opportunity to serve as the GM of UNC Football," Lombardi said in the statement. "I have decided it's best for me to resign my position as GM to allow the team to focus on the '26 season."

The resignation comes five days after the Tar Heels beat TCU 15-10 in Dublin, Ireland , to start Belichick's second season in Chapel Hill. Belichick went 4-8 last year after leading the NFL's New England Patriots to six Super Bowl titles.

Lombardi attended for Belichick's introductory news conference in December 2024, with Belichick announcing that day that the former GM of the NFL's Cleveland Browns would serve as his college-level GM.

A few months into Belichick's tenure, Lombardi said the goal was running a college program in a way similar to the NFL, saying the Tar Heels "consider ourselves the 33rd (NFL) team" because of the staff connections to the pros. That confident statement didn't align with the on-field results; the Tar Heels had more more double-digit losses (five) than wins, along with multiple off-the-field distractions .

Lombardi was given a three-year deal paying him $1.5 million in base salary through the 2027 season. That made him by far the country's highest-paid college football GM for the 2025 season, according to a USA Today salary database, another incongruity with the Tar Heels' results.

At the college level, GMs across sports generally have front-office roles dealing with roster construction and negotiations over player compensation, with the heaviest work coming in the offseason.

Belichick said on July 30 that the team was "working through some things" in adjusting duties to compensate for Lombardi's absence. Roberts said later that day the situation was "distressing to me and everyone else in the administration ... that this is something that we have to have to spend time on."

articles.title: Ex-NLF player, analyst Mark Sanchez to plead guilty in drunken downtown brawl
articles.summary: Mark Sanchez filed a guilty plea Thursday in court and asked the judge to set a sentencing hearing.
articles.body:
INDIANAPOLIS — Former NFL player and Fox Sports analyst Mark Sanchez filed a guilty plea Thursday in his case involving a drunken fight downtown that resulted in Sanchez being stabbed and hospitalized after attacking a 69-year-old man.

Sanchez faced multiple charges after the incident at 12:30 a.m. Oct. 4, including felony battery causing serious bodily injury, battery resulting in bodily injury, unauthorized entry of a motor vehicle and public intoxication.

Sanchez's case was set to go before a jury next week. The details of the plea deal filed in Marion County Superior Court 21 have not been released. IndyStar reached out to Sanchez's attorney, Jennifer Lukemeyer, but did not immediately receive a response.

Sanchez also asked in his filing Thursday that a sentencing hearing be set. The judge in the case has not yet accepted the plea nor set a sentencing.

"This incident brought significant national attention to our city, including false narratives spread by commentators and public officials before the evidence was available," Zachary A. Myers , former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana and a litigation partner with McCarter & English , said in a statement to IndyStar. "Now that Mark Sanchez intends to plead guilty to a crime, the public will want to see whether he will be treated the same as others who commit similar offenses."

Sanchez was in Indy to cover the Indianapolis Colts -Las Vegas Raiders game. The fight began when Sanchez became upset that the 69-year-old man parked his work box truck at a loading dock to collect used cooking oil, court documents state.

Sanchez was stabbed shortly before 12:30 a.m. Oct. 4 in an alleyway near Loughmiller's Pub & Eatery . He suffered stab wounds to his upper torso and was rushed to Eskenazi Hospital in critical condition. Later in the day, he was upgraded to stable condition.

Court documents indicate the 69-year-old man, who suffered a laceration to his left cheek, was defending himself. He was treated and released from Methodist Hospital. Photos of the man shared with IndyStar show him on a hospital bed, bloodied, with a neck brace and a large gash on the left side of his face.

"This incident should never have happened," said Marion County Prosecutor Ryan Mears, at the time. "What began as a disagreement between a 38-year-old former professional athlete and a 69-year-old man should not have escalated into violence or left anyone seriously injured."

Fox Sports fired Sanchez, who came to the network in 2021 as a game analyst, in November and replaced him with Drew Brees.

Sanchez had a 10-year NFL career, four seasons with the New York Jets and time in Philadelphia, Dallas and Washington. He retired in 2019.

articles.title: Ex-NLF player, analyst Mark Sanchez to plead guilty in drunken downtown brawl
articles.summary: Mark Sanchez filed a guilty plea Thursday in court and asked the judge to set a sentencing hearing.
articles.body:
INDIANAPOLIS — Former NFL player and Fox Sports analyst Mark Sanchez filed a guilty plea Thursday in his case involving a drunken fight downtown that resulted in Sanchez being stabbed and hospitalized after attacking a 69-year-old man.

Sanchez faced multiple charges after the incident at 12:30 a.m. Oct. 4, including felony battery causing serious bodily injury, battery resulting in bodily injury, unauthorized entry of a motor vehicle and public intoxication.

Sanchez's case was set to go before a jury next week. The details of the plea deal filed in Marion County Superior Court 21 have not been released. IndyStar reached out to Sanchez's attorney, Jennifer Lukemeyer, but did not immediately receive a response.

Sanchez also asked in his filing Thursday that a sentencing hearing be set. The judge in the case has not yet accepted the plea nor set a sentencing.

"This incident brought significant national attention to our city, including false narratives spread by commentators and public officials before the evidence was available," Zachary A. Myers , former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana and a litigation partner with McCarter & English , said in a statement to IndyStar. "Now that Mark Sanchez intends to plead guilty to a crime, the public will want to see whether he will be treated the same as others who commit similar offenses."

Sanchez was in Indy to cover the Indianapolis Colts-Las Vegas Raiders game. The fight began when Sanchez became upset that the 69-year-old man parked his work box truck at a loading dock to collect used cooking oil, court documents state.

Sanchez was stabbed shortly before 12:30 a.m. Oct. 4 in an alleyway near Loughmiller's Pub & Eatery . He suffered stab wounds to his upper torso and was rushed to Eskenazi Hospital in critical condition. Later in the day, he was upgraded to stable condition.

Court documents indicate the 69-year-old man, who suffered a laceration to his left cheek, was defending himself. He was treated and released from Methodist Hospital. Photos of the man shared with IndyStar show him on a hospital bed, bloodied, with a neck brace and a large gash on the left side of his face.

"This incident should never have happened," said Marion County Prosecutor Ryan Mears, at the time. "What began as a disagreement between a 38-year-old former professional athlete and a 69-year-old man should not have escalated into violence or left anyone seriously injured."

In November, Fox Sports fired Sanchez, who came to the network in 2021 as a game analyst, and replaced him with Drew Brees.

Sanchez had a 10-year NFL career, including four seasons with the New York Jets and time in Philadelphia, Dallas and Washington. He retired in 2019.

articles.title: Alphonso Smith, 2-Time All-America DB Who Played in the NFL for 4 Seasons, Dies at 40
articles.summary: PAHOKEE, Fla. (AP) — Alphonso Smith, a two-time All-America defensive back who played in the NFL for four seasons, has died. He was 40.
articles.body:
PAHOKEE, Fla. (AP) — Alphonso Smith, a two-time All-America defensive back who played in the NFL for four seasons, has died. He was 40.

Smith died on Wednesday, according to Wake Forest , who was informed by his family. The school's release Thursday afternoon didn't reveal a cause of death.

The Associated Press contacted the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in Florida earlier Thursday seeking to confirm Smith's death. In an emailed statement responding to that inquiry, the office said sheriff's deputies had responded to a Pahokee address "in reference to a suicide attempt" on Wednesday afternoon.

"An adult male was transported to the hospital where he succumbed to his injuries," the sheriff's office stated.

EDITOR'S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org

Smith appeared to post on his Facebook account on Wednesday, lamenting his mental health challenges, apologizing and asking for forgiveness.

"Do not cry for me!" a post read on his account. "I tried everything in my power to fight the demons behind the ones that someone put into ME! I did not want to be that WAY! I know I have disappointed so many folks. This is a DEMON in me! But not only me! It's EVERYONE! I have HURT so many! I needed help & did not get it! I am so sorry!"

Smith apologized to his children in the note and suggested that trauma from his childhood had caused him mental anguish.

"I pray my soul rest in heaven for my heart is pure," he said.

Denver drafted the former Wake Forest star in the second round of the 2009 NFL draft. After playing in 15 games for the Broncos, returning punts and kickoffs, he was traded to Detroit shortly before the 2010 season.

Smith played in 33 games, including 11 starts, over the next two seasons with the Lions and had eight interceptions, returning two for touchdowns.

The Lions released him just before the 2012 season, signed him later that year and cut him again after he played in four games as a backup.

Smith went to Pahokee High School in his hometown, where he helped the football team win a Florida state title as a two-way star playing quarterback and defensive back in 2003. He redshirted as a freshman at Wake Forest and went on to become a key player for the program over the next four seasons.

Smith was a first-team AP All-America defensive back in 2008 and a third-team All-America in 2007.

After playing in 44 NFL games over four years, he worked as a sideline reporter for Wake Forest football games during the 2013 season when he was also an assistant high school coach in nearby Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

Smith was a head high school football coach in Moore Haven, Florida, and Pahokee High School, where he was also dean of students in charge of discipline, according to his LinkedIn account. His last listed job was director of marketing for a South Florida family physician.

articles.title: Former NFL star set to plead guilty over Indianapolis altercation
articles.summary: A motion seeks a guilty plea and sentencing hearing in November.
articles.body:
Former NFL quarterback Mark Sanchez is set to plead guilty in connection with an altercation with a truck driver in Indianapolis last year that led to him being stabbed, online court records show.

A motion for a guilty plea and sentencing hearing in the case was filed on Thursday, according to online court records.

The motion requests that the hearing be set in November, according to a spokesperson for the Marion County Prosecutor's Office.

It is unclear what the ex-Fox Sports broadcaster plans to plead guilty to.

He was charged with felony battery in connection with the October 2025 incident, which left him and the truck driver -- Perry Tole -- hospitalized. He was also charged with battery resulting in bodily injury, unauthorized entry of a motor vehicle and public intoxication -- all misdemeanors.

The Marion County Prosecutor's Office spokesperson did not release any additional information.

"Our priority remains securing justice for Mr. Tole," the spokesperson said.

A trial in the case had most recently been scheduled to start on Sept. 8. Tole has also filed a civil suit against Sanchez and Fox Corporation over the incident.

Mark Sanchez's brother and legal adviser, Nick Sanchez Jr., said in a statement Thursday that they are "finalizing an agreement with the prosecutor's office that provides a path toward resolving the state's case."

He said they are also "encouraged by the constructive conversations taking place regarding the related civil matter."

"There is real momentum toward bringing this entire chapter to a close," he said.

An attorney for Tole said in a statement Thursday that they are "pleased with the constructive and professional conversations we've had with Mr. Sanchez's team."

"Our discussions have been productive and we're on a positive path toward an agreement that will allow the parties to move forward," the attorney, Matt Golitko, said. "Mr. Tole appreciates the progress we have achieved and looks forward to an amicable resolution."

The incident occurred shortly after midnight on Oct. 4, 2025, when Sanchez got into a dispute with Tole, who was working at a hotel loading dock, according to police and prosecutors.

Sanchez allegedly climbed into the truck and stopped Tole from calling for help before a fight between the two broke out, according to court records.

Tole's attorney previously told ABC News that the truck driver tried to defend himself by stabbing Sanchez.

Sanchez had several stab wounds to his torso, while Tole suffered a "severe laceration to the side of his face," according to court documents.

At the time, Sanchez was a Fox Sports color commentator and was in the city to broadcast a game between the Las Vegas Raiders and the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium. In the weeks following the incident, a Fox Sports spokesperson confirmed that Sanchez was no longer with the network.

He was a first-round draft pick of the New York Jets in 2009.

articles.title: Judge rules LSU can roster ex-NFL players in defiance of SEC rules ahead of Friday's roster deadline
articles.summary: Will LSU put former NFL players on its roster?
articles.body:
LSU is free to roster players who were on NFL rosters earlier this summer. Will the Tigers actually do it?

Louisiana judge William Jorden ruled in favor of players looking for a fifth year of eligibility and against the SEC after a lengthy proceeding on Thursday. Players like former Ole Miss TE Dae'Quan Harris and former Rebels DT Zxavian Harris were granted a preliminary injunction that allows them to play college football in 2026 even though they were cut from NFL teams.

Both have committed to play for LSU and their former Ole Miss coach Lane Kiffin. And on Friday, LSU has to send its roster for the 2026 season to the SEC. If they or any other players who had signed contracts with NFL teams are on that roster, an even bigger legal fight could unfold.

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry also celebrated the ruling. He played a significant role in the Tigers' pursuit of Kiffin after LSU fired Brian Kelly during the 2025 season.

The SEC filed a lawsuit against Kiffin and LSU earlier in the day in an Alabama federal court. In the wake of the initial Louisiana ruling that gave players from the class of 2022 a fifth year of eligibility even if they had been on an NFL team, the SEC and other power conferences passed rules prohibiting players who had been with NFL teams from playing for a member school.

The conference wants to enforce that rule and cited its First Amendment rights to tell members to comply with the rules in the suit. The league said that Kiffin and LSU "orchestrated a campaign to recruit professional athletes" to play for the Tigers.

It said in a statement Thursday night that it disagreed with Jorden's ruling.

"We disagree with the court's decision," the SEC said. "The SEC's presidents and chancellors unanimously adopted a clear and reasonable standard: member universities should not play former professional athletes on their rosters. The conference and its member universities have the right to establish, through agreed-upon governance procedures, the rules under which they voluntarily compete and to expect those rules to be followed. "The SEC will continue to defend this standard, the principle of fair competition, and the conference's authority to govern competition among its member universities."

"We disagree with the court's decision," the SEC said.

"The SEC's presidents and chancellors unanimously adopted a clear and reasonable standard: member universities should not play former professional athletes on their rosters. The conference and its member universities have the right to establish, through agreed-upon governance procedures, the rules under which they voluntarily compete and to expect those rules to be followed.

"The SEC will continue to defend this standard, the principle of fair competition, and the conference's authority to govern competition among its member universities."

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey testified for multiple hours as part of Thursday's hearing in Louisiana. In his testimony, Sankey defended his conference's right to set and enforce its own rules. His testimony came after Georgia attorney general Chris Carr said in a letter to the SEC on Wednesday that the league should consider taking drastic action against LSU if the Tigers roster a former NFL player.

If LSU doesn't have a player who was on an NFL roster on its own roster on Friday, the potential for a fight isn't necessarily over, either. If the Tigers leave roster spots open — a school can roster up to 105 scholarship players — Kiffin and his coaching staff are free to add players to those open spots as the season goes on. So if LSU doesn't want to test the SEC's wrath ahead of Week 1, it could wait another week or two.

However, it could be testing the limits of that injunction by doing so. As part of his ruling, Jorden enjoined the NCAA, SEC and even LSU from taking action to prevent players from playing.

The whole problem stems from college sports' rampant disorganization in recent years as it's opened the doors for athletes to get paid for NIL deals and also sign revenue-sharing deals with schools. Players like Wright and Harris played four seasons in their four years of college eligibility. But the NCAA announced in June — after the 2026 NFL Draft — that athletes from the class of 2023 onward would immediately have five years to play five seasons.

The timing of the announcement led to multiple lawsuits from players in the class of 2022 who thought they had exhausted their eligibility in the 2025-26 school year.

articles.body: Dianna Russini’s relationship with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel has now led to a clear finding from The Athletic. Recently, the outlet concluded that Russini broke its newsroom standards by failing to disclose the relationship, even though the review found no clear evidence that she used her reporting to help Vrabel or his teams.The finding came after a months-long review of Russini’s work. That wide review gives the latest development more weight than a simple look at her coverage of Vrabel.The Athletic found a disclosure breach involving Dianna Russini and Mike VrabelMike Semel, The Athletic’s editorial director for standards and editorial quality, led the review. His team found that only about 5% of the 903 pieces involved Vrabel, the teams he coached or players those teams pursued. The investigation did not determine the full nature of Dianna Russini and Mike Vrabel’s relationship. articles.title: Here's why, even with all its problems, college football is still better than the NFL
articles.summary: The College Football Playoff's tight 12-team field means week one upsets can derail entire seasons, a pressure the NFL's 14-team format never matches.
articles.body: It's been a tough offseason for college football, with discussions on expanding the College Football Playoff, Lane Kiffin's NFL-to-LSU pipeline, and the ever-expanding crisis of tampering and abuses in the transfer portal or in NIL. While week zero has already come and gone, college football is officially and fully back for week one, starting Thursday evening and continuing without the long Labor Day weekend. And it's a reminder of the many reasons why there's so much more to like and enjoy in the collegiate ranks compared to its big NFL brother. Here's just a few of them. WEEK ONE UPSET SPECIAL: THESE THREE COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS SHOULD BE ON UPSET ALERT THIS WEEKEND These games matter It's the first full week of the season, but with the number of teams in major conferences and the limited spots in the College Football Playoff, each game means something for many programs. A whopping 14 teams reach the postseason in the NFL, out of 32, meaning an incredible 44% of the league makes the playoff. In the NCAA, there are 68 teams between the Big Ten, SEC, ACC, Big 12 and Notre Dame. Just 12 teams reach the College Football Playoff, and one of those spots automatically goes to a Group of 6 team. Not every program in those conferences has realistic hopes of reaching the playoff, but with just 11 spots to go around, just 16.1% of those top teams can play meaningful postseason football. In the 2025 NFL season, for example, the 9-7-1 Green Bay Packers and 8-9 Carolina Panthers made the postseason. Depending on the division or strength of your conference, teams that finish around .500 have a realistic possibility of making the playoffs. Yes, the games "matter," but a loss in week one of the NFL season carries little weight or meaning. In college? It matters. The expanded playoff gives teams room for one or two losses, potentially three this year, depending on schedule, but one slip up in week one can remove any margin for error. Notre Dame in 2025, for example, lost their first game of the season to an eventual playoff team in Miami, lost in week two to another playoff team, Texas A&M, and were left out of the 12-team field. CLEMSON'S DABO SWINNEY THROWS SHADE AT LANE KIFFIN, LSU OVER BRINGING IN NFL PLAYERS: 'IT'S EMBARRASSING' LSU and Clemson both have realistic hopes of reaching the playoffs. And while the loser of Saturday's game isn't eliminated, the path gets harder. Clemson, given their fairly weak schedule, has to beat Miami when the two play next month. LSU plays Ole Miss, Texas A&M, Alabama, Texas, and Tennessee. An early season slip up makes finishing their season with two losses nearly impossible. That's another element to it, upsets matter. Because of the importance of subjective rankings, not objective standings. The Los Angeles Rams are widely expected to be the best team in the NFL this year. If they lose to the New York Giants at home in week two, it doesn't matter more than any other loss in the regular season. Division tiebreakers notwithstanding. ESPN PUTS 20TH RANKED TENNESSEE ON UPSET ALERT, AND YOU'LL NEVER GUESS WHO THEY'RE PLAYING But if Wisconsin beats Notre Dame on Sunday? That changes the season. As unlikely as that outcome is, it's not impossible. Which, once again, makes college football more exciting. Chaos There's no doubt that the NFL offers a higher level of quality football. The players are more athletic, physical, faster, and more developed. Coaching is generally better than at the collegiate level. And the draft ensures that only the best of the best reach NFL training camps and rosters. But therein lies some of the problems. Defenses, in particular, are just too good. The NFL has tried to mitigate some of this obvious disconnect with several rule changes. The new kickoffs have moved field position further up than in years past. Then they started allowing teams to manipulate the actual football that kickers use, the K-ball, allowing them to make increasingly lengthy field goals. With 65–70 yards now a realistic possibility, offenses in the NFL could be in field goal range after picking up just 15–20 yards after a touch back. These changes were clearly made with scoring in mind, because year after year, the offense keeps declining. Those aren't the only rules; the laughable overprotection of quarterbacks was done to ensure that the league's stars stayed healthy and prevent backups from the 6-21 for 76-yard stat line that they're known for. Increasing the focus on illegal contact penalties was also done to give offenses more advantages. While there are a handful of games each year in the NFL that are chaotic and exciting, they're few and far between compared to college. Why? Because college players aren't as good. It's easier to move the ball. Higher scoring games are common. There are dozens of wild, unpredictable comebacks throughout the collegiate ranks. "Pac-12 after dark" became a running joke on social media, before that conference's demise, but the sentiment lives on. Rivalries Yes, the NFL has rivalries, games like Cowboys-Commanders, Packers-Bears, or Chargers-Raiders that have elevated meaning for the fans of both teams. But the importance of those games pales in comparison to traditional college football rivalries. Texas-Oklahoma. USC—UCLA or USC—Notre Dame. Alabama—Auburn. Michigan—Ohio State. Army—Navy. Florida—Georgia. Oregon—Oregon State. Texas—Texas A&M. Florida—Florida State. Utah—BYU. Cal—Stanford. There are many, many more. While it's probably an overstatement to say that a disappointing season can be undone just by beating your rival, but it's not far off. And obviously far exceeds the importance placed on rivalry games in the NFL, playoffs aside. Nobody's getting fired in the NFL based on their record against rivals alone, but an Ohio State coach that can't beat Michigan? Or vice versa? That almost immediately puts them on the hot seat. There are exceptions, of course, like Lambeau Field, Arrowhead, and Lumen Field in Seattle, but is anyone falling over themselves to make a pilgrimage to Mercedes-Benz Stadium? Or MetLife? articles.body:
Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams displayed a new look while attending the Chicago Cubs' 2-1 win over the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday night.

Williams showed off his mustache as he sat alongside Chicago Bulls forwards Caleb Wilson and Matas Buzelis as well as videographer Cole Bennett.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

Williams has developed a friendship with Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong throughout their tenure in Chicago.

"He's my guy," Crow-Armstrong said of Williams on Feb. 12, via SI.com's Matthew Singer . "It's a nice relationship that we're starting to build. Selfishly, it was fun for me to dive into the Bears' season. We both hope and plan to be in Chicago for a long time, so it doesn't hurt to get to know each other and build something. We want to keep the young guys together and connected somehow. That was kind of the start of it. It's been a good start."

Williams is attempting to help the Bears put together another successful season in 2026 after they finished at 11-6 and advanced to the divisional round of the playoffs during their 2025 campaign.

The signal-caller completed 58.1 percent of his throws for 3,942 yards and 27 touchdowns compared to seven interceptions last year.

Meanwhile, Buzelis and Wilson will be crucial building blocks for the Bulls as they try to climb up the Eastern Conference standings.

Buzelis is coming off a 2025-26 season in which he ranked No. 3 among all second-year players by averaging 16.3 points per game. Expectations are also high for Wilson after he was selected with the No. 4 overall pick in the 2026 NBA draft.

As for the Cubs, they improved to 79-62 with Thursday's win and currently own the No. 2 National League Wild Card spot.

articles.title: Dianna Russini faces a clear standards violation after The Athletic’s Mike Vrabel probe, but her NFL reporting escapes a bigger blow
articles.summary: NFL News: The Athletic closed the book on its internal investigation into Dianna Russini on Thursday, nearly five months after photos of the former senior NFL r.
articles.body: The Athletic closed the book on its internal investigation into Dianna Russini on Thursday, nearly five months after photos of the former senior NFL reporter and New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel surfaced on Page Six. The outlet's editorial director for standards and quality, Mike Semel, reviewed 903 stories, 77 videos, and 204 podcast episodes tied to Russini's 32-month tenure. The conclusion: a clear standards violation for failing to disclose her relationship with Vrabel, but no evidence that her reporting was compromised.What did The Athletic's investigation into Dianna Russini actually find?Semel's review determined that Dianna Russini's undisclosed alleged relationship with Vrabel represented a "clear violation" of the outlet's standards. But the violation was procedural, not editorial. Of the 903 stories reviewed, only 46 written pieces mentioned Vrabel or the Patriots at all, and just three videos were related to the coach directly.The report's harshest finding was about disclosure, not bias. "Russini's relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic's standards," the report states. "Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed."Semel was even more specific: "Russini should have disclosed to The Athletic the nature of her relationship with Vrabel to allow editors to assess the kinds of stories on which she should have been working, if any. She did not."That failure to disclose is the central issue. Not fabricated quotes, not planted stories, not favorable scoops orchestrated to advance Vrabel's public image. Just a relationship that, by The Athletic's own standards, should have been flagged to editors so they could make the call on her assignments. That's a meaningful distinction, and one the investigation was careful to draw.On the substance of her work, Semel was measured but not damning. "Most of what Russini wrote about Vrabel or the Patriots was transactional and newsy," Semel wrote. "In addition, I've not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic."He did flag some pieces where the tone around Vrabel read as "awkward or even uncomfortable" in hindsight, while also acknowledging that nearly all media coverage of Vrabel's return to New England was similarly glowing at the time. That context matters. It limits how far you can stretch the criticism.Russini, who resigned in April, was not subject to a personal conduct probe given she was no longer employed at the outlet. Her response was brief. "I stand by any and all reporting I've ever done in my career," she told Andrew Marchand.Will Dianna Russini return to NFL reporting after the scandal?The investigation does not answer that question, but those close to Russini seem to think the door is open. Former NFL insider Mike Silver said: "I do think she's going to be back, probably not as an insider, at least in the short term. But I think she'll be back in this realm, probably talking about football and other things pretty soon."What makes Silver's read interesting is what it implies. Russini's credibility as a reporter was not gutted by this report. A full finding of bias or inaccuracy would have been career-ending. Instead, The Athletic confirmed a disclosure failure and stopped well short of anything worse.The investigation did not attempt to define the relationship itself, with Semel noting: "We neither completed an investigation nor reached any conclusion about the nature of the full relationship between Vrabel and Russini, but the totality of the public photographs are enough to conclude a violation of company policy."That leaves a lot unresolved. The report was thorough in scope but narrow in what it could actually determine. With the Patriots opening the 2026 NFL season against the Seahawks in a Super Bowl 60 rematch, attention now shifts back to Vrabel on the sideline. Whether Russini eventually chooses to speak publicly in detail remains the one development that could reopen this story in any meaningful way.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
